docs.title: Second Sun
docs.text:
Find a planet around two suns. The whole project in one line. We search NASA's TESS light for a planet that circles two stars at once. Finding one is a win, and so is proving, with measured numbers, that none was there to find.

Now: 17 Nov 2026, 8:45 pm: Fable's leftover jobs are done. New rule: a freeze may not add many real alarms with no upside-down twin; that sinks Fable's candidate (mask timing M2 and the dump rule both fail it). Best safe change, C3 (two more holds released): +2.7 points, but only +1.6 on fresh planets, under the +2.0 bar, so nothing freezes yet. Orbit search (X9) adds 0 planets. P stays 48%; 0.75 is far. Ahmed decides: lower the bar or not.

How well we see

Our search tool, Petrova. Every branch here is a way a real planet could slip past it, ordered by how many test planets each one loses.

  • Found, but held back (1.1, next): The tool finds the dip but a safety flag keeps it from the top tier. The biggest fixable loss on our test bench.
  • Outside the searched windows (1.2, next): The planet's dip falls in a stretch of data the search never looks at, so it cannot be found at all.
  • The dip is missed (1.3, active): The detector itself does not see the dip, usually because it is too shallow for the noise around it.
  • The eclipse mask hides the transit (1.4, active): We blank out the binary's own eclipses before searching. If those blanks are too wide or in the wrong place, they swallow the planet too.
  • Blind spot for fast binaries (1.5, next): Binaries that orbit each other in 5 to 10 days are noisier, and the tool finds very few test planets around them.
  • False alarms (1.6, parked): The other side of every fix. A change that finds more planets but also more fake ones is no gain. The upside-down test light counts the fake ones.
  • The scoreboard (1.7, done): The fixed test of 2,000 planted planets that decides whether any change to the tool counts.
Where we look

Which stars we search, and the data we search them in.

  • Census (2.1, waits): A list of eclipsing binaries we build ourselves from newer TESS data, so our searches reach stars nobody has searched this way.
  • G1 (2.2, waits): 552 Kepler binaries that TESS also watched. Searched only once, sealed, after the tool is fixed and frozen.
  • Data and downloads (2.3, parked): Getting the light files from NASA's archive and keeping them complete and correct.
  • Ideas on hold (2.4, parked): Bigger systems we designed but parked until the main search is done.
How we prove it

The rules and statistics that keep us honest, so a result means what it says.

  • Statistics and controls (3.1, parked): How we decide that a signal is more than chance, using the upside-down light as a fair comparison.
  • Records and tests (3.2, parked): Every run leaves a record that lets anyone repeat it, and every tool has tests that can fail.
  • Leads (3.3, parked): The steps a promising dip must pass, with two independent checks and your yes, before we ever call it a planet.
  • Going public later (3.4, parked): How and when a result would be shared with astronomers, once there is something to share.
Tools and book

The book, the textbook, and the pages and tools around the search.

  • Book and learning (4.1, active): This book and its textbook, built so you can follow and check everything we do.
  • Search window and control room (4.2, waits): The live page that shows a search while it runs.
  • Machine and housekeeping (4.3, parked): The computer, the scripts and the small repairs that keep the work running.
  • Eyes pages (4.4, parked): The practice pages where you learn to tell real dips from fake ones.

docs.title: Candidates
docs.text:
In plain words

A candidate is a dip that passed our first checks. It is not a planet. Each one gets an ID (SS-0001, SS-0002, ...) and, once it survives vetting, a nickname. It needs two keys before it goes anywhere: my analysis, and your own check.

docs.title: Claims register
docs.text:
In plain words

Ahmed, every fact the book relies on lives here once, with how sure we are and where it came from. Pages show a small label next to a fact; tap it and you land on its row here.

docs.title: How to read the labels
docs.text: The shape carries the meaning, not the colour. VERIFIED (solid outline) means we read the original source or measured it ourselves. LIKELY (dashed) means a summary or secondary source. UNVERIFIED (dotted) means memory or one weak source: test before relying on it.

docs.title: Eyes mode
docs.text:
Hunt · practice and the official test · every answer saved

The story

In the first six quarters of Kepler data, volunteers on a website called Planet Hunters found a planet by looking at light curves by eye. It crosses the larger of two stars, which circle each other every 20 days, about once every 137 days, and it was named PH1 b VERIFIED. A second pair of stars, about 1,000 times the Earth-Sun distance away, makes it the first transiting planet known in a four-star system VERIFIED. Ahmed, that is why this book has an eyes mode: some planets have been found by people looking.

In plain words

You get a short stretch of real light curve with nothing marked on it. Say Dip, No dip, Odd or Not sure. After every answer a big banner says what it truly was: a dip, or not a dip and why. Every answer is saved on your device, so your scores are kept. It is practice and a test: the dips are fake planets we hid, plus glitches and real eclipses that we know about.

With JavaScript on, this spot is a practice game: you look at short stretches of the real TOI-1338 light curve and say whether you see a dip.

How it works
  • Look for a dip that comes back up. Choose Dip, No dip, Odd or Not sure.
  • Practice reveals the truth after each answer. Tests reveal it at the end.
  • Answers are locked and saved after every card. Use Review to look back.
  • Standard, hard and rehearsal results each have their own pass line.
Full guidance and test rules
  • Blind first. Nothing is marked until you answer, then the hidden thing is outlined.
  • Four answers. Dip is a planet-like dip that comes back up. No dip means nothing there. Odd is something that is not a planet: an eclipse, a spike or a sudden jump. Not sure is always allowed, and it is honest.
  • The banner tells you the truth. After each answer in practice it says THIS WAS: A DIP or THIS WAS: NOT A DIP, what it was, and whether you were right. If you said No dip to an eclipse, it says you were right that it is not a dip, but that it was an eclipse.
  • What the numbers say. In practice, and in the review after a test, three short lines are worked out from the dots of that very curve: how strong its best dip is on the hunt's own scale (7 or more is what the hunt keeps), how it compares with the next best wiggle, whether it ends at a hole in the data, whether the level jumps and stays, and so on. Every number in them was measured on that curve, the three lines are always about the same length, and the wording rotates so you do not read the same sentence twice. The lines pick what to say from the measurements alone, never from the hidden answer. The answer only decides the last line: what it was, and what to check next time. When a curve comes close to a known artifact pattern without crossing its line, the lines say it is not classified instead of calling it plain noise.
  • A line on the plot. After you answer in practice, a dashed line shows how deep a dip must be, over the best stretch of that curve, to score 7. A solid line shows how deep that stretch really is. You can see at a glance whether it reaches the hunt's bar.
  • Twin drill (in Hard mode). Two curves with exactly the same noise: one hides a faint fake planet (strength 5 to 8.5), the other has none. You say Top, Bottom or Not sure, then it shows the measured strength of both. It is not saved, not sent anywhere and does not count towards any line, so it is pure practice for the hardest confusion: telling a faint planet from noise that looks the same.
  • A miss comes back. In practice, when you get a curve wrong, a curve of the same kind is moved to 3 to 5 curves later (the sitting keeps exactly the same curves). Tests are never reordered.
  • Your habit by strength. My results shows, for the curves measured since this was added, how often you said Dip at each strength (under 3, 3 to 5, 5 to 7, 7 to 10, 10 or more), the strength from which you say Dip on more than half of the curves, and your d-prime and criterion. The hunt's line is 7, so the table shows whether your own line is higher or lower.
  • Look back, read only. Press Look at previous question (or the left arrow) to see an earlier curve and what you answered. You can never change an answer.
  • Keys. On a keyboard, press 1 to 4 to answer and Enter for the next one. Left and right arrows look back and forward, Escape returns.
  • Practice sittings of 5, 20, 50 or 100 light curves show the answer after every curve.
  • The official test is 30 curves (10 clear dips, 4 faint ones, 8 quiet, 8 odd things) with no answers until the end. It counts towards the pass line: at least 85% of the clear dips found and at most 1 in 10 quiet curves called a dip, over at least 60 curves, in at least 2 rounds, on at least 2 different days. The faintest dips are reported but are not part of the line. Claude decides, from your results, when you are ready.
  • The HARD test (step two of the ladder to real data) is 30 curves with its own line, kept apart from the official one. Its cards are harder on purpose. The "nothing hidden" cards are not random stretches: each is the best-looking dip found in a whole sector of fresh noise made from this star's own noise, which is what the hunt hands you. Half of them are shaped like a planet's dip (as long as a fake planet), the other half are the natural kind, because real noise peaks are short. Its fake planets are 3 to 12 hours long and go down to the edge of what anyone can see. Strength is the hunt's own box score, measured on the finished curve (about 10 to 14 for the clear ones, 4 to 9 for the near-limit ones; the hunt keeps 7 and above). Hard noise scores about 4.5 in the middle and roughly 1 curve in 6 reaches 7 or more. The odd things include dips that end at a gap in the data (the classic thruster artifact), jumps down that never recover, and subtle spikes. The mix is 6 clear fake planets, 6 near the limit, 8 hard-noise cards and 10 odd things. Not sure is a fair answer on the hardest cards and is free there, but on a clear fake planet it counts as a miss. The line, fixed before it was first played: at least 80% of the clear fake planets found and at most 20% of the hard-noise cards called a dip, over at least 4 hard rounds, 120 curves and 2 different days. Hard practice shows the answer after every curve.
  • The rehearsal (step three of the ladder) has its own page, Rehearsal: the layout the real candidates will use, with fake planets hidden among real eclipses, flares, steps and instrument effects. Its own line is written there. Its rounds are saved and sent like these, but counted apart.
  • Your results are saved after every answer, on this device, and a round you leave half done is kept as abandoned, then sent to the cloud like the others. The My results button shows every round: right, wrong, not sure, dips found and false alarms. You never have to send anything to Claude: the moment you finish a round (or leave one half done), it is sent by itself to a private cloud copy. If you were offline, it waits on your phone and goes the moment the internet is back. A line under the results says so ("all 3 finished rounds are safe in the cloud, and Claude can read them"). Add this book to your phone's Home Screen so the phone keeps your rounds while they wait.
  • Practice only for now. Every stretch comes from the real TOI-1338 light curve (TESS sector 98) with answers we know. The real candidates of the hunt get their own tab here once Claude agrees your results are good enough.
  • Looking exercise. This page has no text version, because the skill is seeing the picture. The light-curve explorer in Chapter 2 and the numbers in Chapter 7 cover the same ideas in words.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Every technical word in the book, in plain words. Pages link here the first time they use a term.

docs.title: Aperture
docs.text: The group of pixels whose light is added up to make a star's light curve. Choosing it well keeps the star's light in and the neighbours' light out. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Aperture loss
docs.text: Light from the star that falls outside the aperture, so the star looks fainter than it is. When TESS's pointing wobbles (worst just before a momentum dump) the star's image smears and some light spills out: a dip that only ever goes down. See the 14 Nov 2026 field note.

docs.title: Arcsecond
docs.text: A tiny angle: 1/3,600 of a degree. A TESS pixel covers 21 arcseconds. Written ″; an arcminute (′) is 60 of them. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Binary star
docs.text: Two stars held together by gravity, each circling their shared centre. Our hunting ground: pairs where a planet might orbit both. See Chapter 4.

docs.title: Biweight filter
docs.text: A way to draw a smooth line through a light curve that ignores dips and outliers, so slow trends can be divided out without erasing a transit. Our detector uses a 2-day one. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: BTJD
docs.text: The TESS clock, in days: Barycentric Julian Date minus 2,457,000. BTJD 4025.6 is 16 December 2025.

docs.title: Cadence
docs.text: One measurement in a light curve, or the time between measurements: 2 minutes for SPOC light curves, 200 seconds for today's full-frame images.

docs.title: Candidate
docs.text: A dip in a light curve that passed our first checks and might be a planet. Not a planet until professionals confirm it.

docs.title: CDPP
docs.text: "Combined Differential Photometric Precision": NASA's estimate of how much a star's brightness wobbles over a given time (like 1 hour), stored in each light-curve file. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Centroid
docs.text: The centre of a star's light on the camera, like the balance point of its pixels. If it shifts during a dip, the dip may come from a neighbour. See Chapter 10.

docs.title: Circumbinary planet
docs.text: A planet that orbits both stars of a pair. Its dips come at irregular times, which is why standard searches miss them. Our main quest.

docs.title: Common moment
docs.text: A flag from version 7. A dip is doubtful if three or more other stars on the same camera have an event of either kind (a dip or an upside-down dip) within 0.1 days. It replaced the older burst flag, which counted only upside-down events and so treated the control differently from the data. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Completeness
docs.text: The share of real planets a search would catch, measured by hiding fake planets in real data and counting how many come back. Ours keeps about 83 in 100 strong ones through the flags. See Chapter 9.

docs.title: Control
docs.text: A test run where the right answer is known to be "nothing", to see how many false alarms the method makes. Ours is the upside-down light curve. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Critical orbit
docs.text: The closest a planet can orbit a pair of stars and stay stable: usually 2.5 to 3.5 times the stars' separation. See Chapter 4.

docs.title: CTOI
docs.text: Community TESS Object of Interest: a planet candidate found by a team outside NASA, posted on ExoFOP. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text: How much of the star's light a dip blocks, as a fraction: depth = (planet radius ÷ star radius)². Usually given in % or ppm.

docs.title: Detached binary
docs.text: Two stars far enough apart that they don't touch or distort each other; their eclipses look like clean, separate dips. Our G1 list keeps only these (Kepler's "morph" value below 0.5).

docs.title: Detrending
docs.text: Removing slow drifts (from the star or the spacecraft) so short dips stand out. We divide by a smooth fitted curve with a 2-day window. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Dominated
docs.text: A dip is dominated when the strongest upside-down dip in the same light curve is at least as strong. A fair local contest, with no setting to tune. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Eclipse overlap
docs.text: A flag for a dip that falls inside one of the two stars' own eclipses, where it is the stars and not a planet. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Eclipsing binary
docs.text: Two stars orbiting each other, lined up so that one passes in front of the other. Makes deep, regular dips.

docs.title: ExoFOP
docs.text: The website where astronomers share follow-up information on TESS planet candidates. Since 2026 it asks for a published paper before accepting a community candidate. See Chapter 14.

docs.title: False alarm
docs.text: A "detection" caused by noise or spacecraft effects instead of a real dip. We count them by searching upside-down data.

docs.title: FITS
docs.text: The standard file format of astronomy since 1981: a header of labels plus tables or images. Every TESS file is FITS. See Lab 2.

docs.title: Flag
docs.text: A reason to doubt a dip. We flag and sort dips, we never delete them. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Flat-baseline test
docs.text: A transit is a box: the light just before and after it is normal. A dip whose two sides are not level, or that has no data on one side, is a ramp, a cliff or a data edge. Also called the step test. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Frozen settings
docs.text: Every setting and a fingerprint of every file written down before any result is read, so the rules cannot be tuned to the answer. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Full-frame image (FFI)
docs.text: A picture of a TESS camera's whole view, saved every 30 minutes, 10 minutes or 200 seconds depending on the year. Every star in view is in it. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Gaia
docs.text: The European Space Agency's star-mapping spacecraft. Its catalogue gives positions, distances and colours for over a billion stars. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Heavy tails
docs.text: Real noise makes far more very big wobbles than bell-curve noise would, so a 7 sigma dip is not as rare as the maths says. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Injection test
docs.text: Hiding computer-made planet dips of known size in real data and checking how many the search finds. It measures what we can and can't detect.

docs.title: Kepler
docs.text: NASA's space telescope that stared at one patch of sky from 2009 to 2013 and found thousands of planets and eclipsing binaries. Our G1 stars come from its binary catalogue. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: KIC
docs.text: Kepler Input Catalog number: Kepler's ID for a star, like KIC 12644769 for Kepler-16.

docs.title: Light curve
docs.text: A star's brightness measured again and again over time and drawn as a graph: time along the bottom, brightness up the side.

docs.title: Look-elsewhere effect
docs.text: If you search in thousands of places, a few will show something unusual by chance. A search's false-alarm rate must count all its tries. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Lopsided noise
docs.text: Noise that is not the same upwards and downwards: flares and glitches jump up more than down, so an upside-down light curve makes more false dips than a real one. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Magnitude
docs.text: Astronomy's brightness scale, where bigger numbers are fainter. 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: MAST
docs.text: The Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes: NASA's public archive holding all TESS and Kepler data. See Lab 1.

docs.title: Matched filter
docs.text: Sliding a template shaped like the signal you want (for us, a box-shaped dip) along the data and scoring how well each stretch matches.

docs.title: Momentum dump
docs.text: A short thruster firing that TESS uses every few days to stay pointed. It jolts the camera and can fake a dip; it's flagged in the data (quality bit 32). See Lab 2.

docs.title: N-body simulation
docs.text: A computer calculation that moves several objects (like two stars and a planet) step by step under each other's gravity. STANLEY uses one to predict when a two-star planet crosses.

docs.title: Orbit-start ramp
docs.text: TESS settles and scattered light is strongest just after it resumes recording, which fakes slow dips. We doubt every dip within 1 day after data resumes. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: Parsec
docs.text: A distance of about 3.26 light years, used by astronomers. Kepler-16 is 75 parsecs away.

docs.title: PDCSAP and SAP
docs.text: Two versions of NASA's light curves. SAP is the raw light summed in the star's pixels; PDCSAP has known spacecraft effects removed.

docs.title: Phase fold
docs.text: Cutting a light curve into pieces one period long and stacking them, so repeating events (like eclipses) line up. Our eclipse mask finds eclipses this way.

docs.title: Photon noise
docs.text: The natural wobble in counting particles of light: like raindrops in a bucket, a count of N varies by about √N. It's the floor no instrument can beat. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: ppm
docs.text: Parts per million. 1% = 10,000 ppm. Earth crossing the Sun blocks about 84 ppm.

docs.title: Precession
docs.text: The slow turning of a planet's orbit around a pair of stars. It makes transits switch on and off over years. See Chapter 5.

docs.title: QLP
docs.text: MIT's Quick-Look Pipeline: makes light curves from full-frame images for a huge number of stars. All 549 G1 stars have QLP data. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Quality flag
docs.text: A number stored with each measurement that warns about problems (thruster firing, scattered light...). 0 means fine. See Lab 2.

docs.title: RA and Dec
docs.text: The sky's longitude (Right Ascension) and latitude (Declination). Every star's address. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Radius
docs.text: Distance from the centre of a star or planet to its edge. We measure planets in Earth radii and stars in Sun radii (the Sun is about 109 Earths wide).

docs.title: Red noise
docs.text: Slow wobbles where neighbouring measurements move together. Unlike random noise, it doesn't shrink much when you average, so it fakes planet-like dips. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Repeater
docs.text: A star with three or more dips in one sector. A planet around two stars cannot make that many in 27 days, so it is a variable star or a second eclipsing pair. See Chapter 10.

docs.title: Robust spread
docs.text: A measure of wobble that ignores a few wild points: 1.4826 times the median distance from the median. Our detector uses it everywhere. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Scattered light
docs.text: Sunlight bounced off Earth or the Moon into TESS's cameras, raising the background. It creates slow ramps and fake dips, usually near the ends of each orbit.

docs.title: Secondary eclipse
docs.text: When the brighter star passes in front of the fainter one: a shallower dip than the primary eclipse, at another point in the binary's orbit.

docs.title: Sector
docs.text: One TESS stretch of about 27 days looking at the same patch of sky.

docs.title: SNR
docs.text: Signal-to-noise ratio: how big a signal is compared with normal wobble. SNR 7 means seven times the normal wobble. Our detection bar is 7.

docs.title: SPOC
docs.text: NASA's Science Processing Operations Center: makes the cleanest TESS light curves, from 2-minute postage stamps. See Chapter 3.

docs.title: Stability limit
docs.text: The closest a planet can orbit a pair of stars without being thrown out, about 3.7 binary periods for equal stars. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: STANLEY
docs.text: A search tool by David Martin's group (Martin et al. 2021) that looks for two-star planets by simulating orbits and stacking all their predicted crossings together. Installed on your PC.

docs.title: TESS
docs.text: NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, launched in 2018. It photographs most of the sky, one sector at a time. All its data is free.

docs.title: TIC
docs.text: TESS Input Catalog number: TESS's ID for a star, like TIC 299096355 for Kepler-16. See Chapter 1.

docs.title: Tier
docs.text: A bin for a dip after our flags: 1A, 1L and 1B are the unflagged ones (candidates could only come from there), tier 2 is flagged, tier 3 disagrees with a second data product. See Chapter 8.

docs.title: TOI
docs.text: TESS Object of Interest: a signal NASA's team thinks might be a planet. TOI-1338 became TOI-1338 b once confirmed.

docs.title: Transit
docs.text: A planet passing in front of its star as seen from Earth, which makes a small dip in the light curve.

docs.title: Virtual environment
docs.text: A private copy of Python with its own toolkits, kept inside a project folder so it doesn't clash with anything else. Ours is D:\second-sun\.venv. See Lab 0.

docs.title: White noise
docs.text: Random wobble where each measurement is independent. Averaging N measurements shrinks it by √N. See Chapter 7.

docs.title: Rehearsal: the real layout
docs.text:
Hunt · step three of the ladder to real data · every answer saved

In plain words

This is the dress rehearsal. Real candidates will be shown to you in exactly this layout, so you practise on it first. Each item is a stretch of real TESS light with at most one thing hidden in it. You look, say what you think it is, lock your answer, and only then see the truth. About three items in ten hide a fake planet. The rest are eclipses, instrument effects, flares, steps, or nothing at all.

With JavaScript on, this spot is the rehearsal: eight sessions of 20 items each.

How it works
  • Look at the whole sector, the event up close and its place in the binary orbit.
  • Choose an answer and optionally your confidence, then lock it to see the truth.
  • Every locked answer is saved. Back to the start returns to the session controls.
Full guidance and test rules
  • Three panels, the same every time. Panel 1 is the whole sector of light, with the binary's eclipses shaded grey and the event shown as a highlighted column. Panel 2 is the event up close, on a fixed scale (the same for every item of a star), with a faint line for every 6 minutes and a bold line for every 30 minutes. Panel 3 shows where the event falls in the binary's orbit.
  • Six answers. Planet-like, Eclipse, Flare, Instrumental, Step, and Unclear (nothing there, or you cannot tell). No answer is pre-selected. You can say how sure you are, then you lock.
  • Lock, then truth. A locked answer cannot be changed. The truth is shown with what was hidden and how deep it was, and whether you called it planet-like correctly.
  • No names, no numbers. Nothing on the screen says which star it is, and nothing tells you in advance what the hunt's own score was. Only the picture.
  • What the hidden things are. Fake planets are planted into real light (three clearly visible and three near the limit in every session). Eclipses are the real eclipses of the binary. Instrument effects are a ramp after a data gap or a dip that ends where the data stop. A flare brightens fast and fades slowly. A step is a level change that stays. "Nothing hidden" items are the best wiggle the hunt's own search finds in another part of the sector.
  • The line. Over eight sessions on at least four different days: at least 80% of the clearly visible fake planets called planet-like, at most 15% of everything else called planet-like, and a d-prime of at least 2. The numbers were written down before this page existed. Claude decides whether your results are enough; the page only does the arithmetic.
  • Saved after every answer, on this device, and sent by itself to the private cloud copy like the other Eyes rounds. A session you leave half done is kept as abandoned.

docs.title: Honest limits of this first version
docs.text:
• Only panels 1 to 3 are here. The second light-curve product, background and centroid panels come in a later version.
  • The fake planets are trapezoids planted into real light. A real planet's shape may differ a little, so a good result here is necessary, not sufficient.
  • There are eight sessions of 20. After the eighth, the same items come round again, so use the later rounds for habit, not for the line.
  • A gap in the window is a real cue: instrument effects sit next to gaps, and the hunt itself would never keep an event next to a gap as a candidate.
  • Everything shown is real light from binaries we used for tuning. No candidate and no event of the hunt appears here.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The light at the top is green and pulsing when numbers are arriving and search processes are running. Amber: the exporter is up but no search process is found. Red: no new numbers for a few minutes. A ring with no fill: a campaign is prepared and has not started; nothing is running and nothing moves until Ahmed gives the word.
  • Three campaigns so far. Re-search 1 (Petrova 1.0.0) searches the light that the old Vesper filter threw away in slow binary stars (5 days or longer). It uses only stars that were not looked at while the new filter was designed: 803 stars from the G2 and G3 lists, in two parts. The 549 Kepler-field stars (G1) follow later, once their eclipse widths are sourced and tested. It ran on 11 Nov 2026 (about 25 minutes) and is finished and scored: result NO EXCESS, no leads; the numbers are in the 11 Nov field note. It was blind: real and upside-down dips were pooled, and no pictures or star lists are shown. G3 (Vesper 0.8.1, 612 stars) ran on 4 Nov 2026 and is finished and scored (result NO EXCESS; the numbers are in the 4 Nov field note): open the finished G3 run. The page shows it counts only, with no pictures and no star list. G2 sealed (Vesper 0.8.0, 594 stars, scored 30 Oct 2026, result NO EXCESS) is kept as it was published: open the finished G2 sealed run. That copy includes its pictures and the star details Ahmed allowed on 30 Oct.
  • "What the search found" sits right under the light. It starts with one plain verdict, then a funnel from all dips to leads, real beside upside-down. A lead is a star with a confirmed real dip and no known planet, one card per star, with the checks done, the checks waiting, and the next one. The rules were written before any sealed result was read (LEADS-RULES.md in the project).
  • Every star goes through the same path. The step that is working glows.
  • Every dip is tested against all the safety checks. The page lists eight of them and files each dip under the first listed one that fired, so the rows add up and are not independent counts. Most dips are filed under the spacecraft-settling check, because that is where TESS data is worst. Two further checks (burst, and orbit-locked in the final report) are not listed yet.
  • Tier 1 is the group we keep: dips with no known innocent cause. It is a list to study, not a list of planets.
  • The self-test pastes fake planets into every star-sector and checks that the machine still sees them.

In plain words

This page shows the search while it runs: how many stars are done, what each safety check stopped, pictures of real dips as they are found (not in the blind G3 run), and a self-test with fake planets. The pictures are real TESS light, there so you can learn what a stopped dip and a kept dip look like. I do not look at each star by eye; every star goes through exactly the same checks, and this page lets you watch them work.

docs.title: Field notes
docs.text:
Records · one lesson per working day

In plain words

After every working session, what we did goes here as a short lesson, the same day. If you've been away, read the notes since your last visit, newest at the bottom of the list. This is the rule from 20 October: nothing we do stays only in the chat.

Each note has the same parts: in plain words · what we did and why · the idea behind it (with links to the chapters) · how you could do it yourself · what we found, and what we didn't · one or two questions.

Date Main lesson 19 October 2026 How a research project starts: what's known, where the gap is, and measuring before deciding 20 October 2026 Testing honestly: fake planets, false alarms, a bug in a professional tool, and Compass 21 October 2026 A progress bar that has to prove itself: evidence, auto-counting and logged changes 23 October 2026 Rebuilding the book around a map: orientation, optional labs and a real-sky home page 24 October 2026 Feedback that is measured, not copied: one strength score, cards that stop giving themselves away, and breaking the code on purpose 27 October 2026 Measure the advice before you take it: contrast numbers, a font file's character list, one learning path, and a plain score line 28 October 2026 Check the rival before you copy it: a professional tool, its licence, how few stars we truly share, and how faint a dip our own search can see 29 October 2026 How small a planet could we have found? Fake dips through the whole chain, a mislabelled half, and a guess that was seven times off 30 October 2026 Why the filter will not improve for free: a rule written first, stacking skipped, and a box floor that only moved the false alarms 31 October 2026 The search did see the known planet: our test used an old calendar. Flares, the price of each safety check, and counting in stars instead of events 2 November 2026 Compare like with like: a consistency check stopped a comparison against an older run made under different conditions; the rehearsal for real candidates went live 3 November 2026 When a frozen version refuses to freeze, believe it: five files had moved the fingerprint, a test (not the code) caused two mismatches, and text on the phone got a 14 px floor 4 November 2026 The G3 search ran once and found nothing: what a clean null is, why it is not the same as no planets, and why 'no excess' can still show fewer real dips than noise 10 November 2026 Our eclipse mask was deleting planets and our tests could not see it: what the audit found, how we measured it, and what every floor number in the book now means 11 November 2026 We searched the hidden light again, found nothing, and learned how to read a null 14 November 2026 The spacecraft's own hiccups make fake dips, and a fairness check that only sees bumps cannot catch them

docs.title: 19 October 2026: how a research project starts
docs.text:
Field note · day 1 · about 8 min

In plain words

We didn't touch a single light curve until we knew three things: what's already been found, where nobody has looked, and whether the data is good enough to look there. That took the whole day, and it decided our first campaign: G1, Kepler's two-star systems re-watched by TESS.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Set the rules first. 25 rounds of questions fixed what we hunt, how sure we must be before calling something a candidate, and which decisions are yours. Rules made before the data can't be bent to fit the data.
  2. Census of what's known. Only 14 transiting two-star planets are known: 12 from Kepler and 2 from TESS VERIFIED. That's a tiny club, so even one new member would matter.
  3. Gap check. Where hasn't anyone looked? Normal planet searches look for dips that repeat on a timetable. Two-star planets break the timetable (Chapter 5), so they're under-searched in TESS data.
  4. Measured the data before choosing. I downloaded real files and measured their size VERIFIED and their noise. A quick estimate said one hour of Kepler-16's data wobbles by only 236 parts per million VERIFIED. Corrected on 20 October: that quick method was too optimistic; measured the way our search sees the data it's about 900 ppm VERIFIED (Chapter 7). The decision still stood, because the injection test measured what we can actually find.
  5. Chose G1. Kepler found thousands of eclipsing binaries VERIFIED. Two-star planets' orbits slowly tilt ("precess"), so their transits switch on and off over years VERIFIED. A planet that was "off" during Kepler could be "on" now in TESS. You approved it from your phone.
  6. Founded this book, with your rule: professional, clean, not gamey.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
• A research gap is a question nobody has answered with the data that exists. Ours: has anyone searched TESS data of Kepler's binaries for single, irregular transits? The census and the reading said: not systematically.
  • Measure, don't guess. "Is TESS good enough?" was answered with a number from a real file, not an opinion. You'll see this rule all through the book.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• The census: NASA's Exoplanet Archive lets anyone list known planets. We asked for every planet flagged as orbiting two stars.
  • The noise: in Lab 2 you download the same kind of file. Chapter 7 shows how to measure its noise.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Found: a clear campaign (G1), a measured data budget, and a list of rivals to watch.
  • Not yet: any searching. Day 1 was all preparation, on purpose.
  • One thing went wrong: timed helper sessions froze on a permission prompt about 10 seconds after starting, so the research continued in the main session. Lesson: test automation before trusting it overnight.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why decide the rules before looking at any data?

So the data can't bend them. If you set the bar after seeing a signal, it's too easy to set it just below that signal.

2. Why might a planet missed by Kepler be visible to TESS?

Its orbit slowly tilts (precesses). Transits switch on and off over years, so it may have been "off" during Kepler (2009 to 2013) and "on" since.

docs.title: 20 October 2026: testing honestly
docs.text:
Field note · night 1 and morning · about 12 min

Correction, 10 Nov 2026

An audit found that our fake-planet tests added the fake dips after the step that hides eclipses, or used a mask built from clean light. A real planet's dip is already in the light when that step runs, and the step can delete it. With the fakes put in first, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips, and the loss grows as the binary gets slower (most lost dips are in 5 to 14 day binaries, because most of our data are there). So every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor" number on this page is an upper limit. "No excess of real dips over noise" is not changed. The full story.

In plain words

Overnight we built a better planet search and then spent most of our effort trying to break it: hiding fake planets to see which it finds, flipping the data upside down to count false alarms, and running it on a real G1 star. In the morning, a bug in the professionals' tool (STANLEY) was found and worked around, and we measured our search with fake planets that move like real ones. No new planet. But we now know what our search can and can't see.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. Detector version 2. It slides a box of 3 to 15 hours along the light curve and asks "is it darker in here than usual?" (Chapter 8). It re-found TOI-1338 b in 4 of 8 sectors VERIFIED.
  2. Fake planets. We added made-up transits of known sizes and checked which were found: down to about 6 Earth radii LIKELY.
  3. Upside-down data. Flip the light curve (2 − brightness) and any dip becomes a bump. Whatever the search still "finds" must be noise: 6 fakes in 10 sectors VERIFIED.
  4. A failed clean-up. Throwing out dips near spacecraft events removed fakes but also half the real crossings. So those became warning flags for a human (Chapter 10).
  5. A timing check. A 2024 paper predicted a TOI-1338 b crossing on 16 December 2025. We found it VERIFIED, 56 ± 5 minutes after the predicted time.
  6. G1 frozen, QLP fixed, auto eclipse finder, Kepler-16 dry run. The one dip on Kepler-16 was the telescope wobbling before a thruster firing. Nothing survived.
  7. STANLEY installed and run (Chapter 12). Its strongest signal was near 96 days (first misread as 94; corrected in the afternoon), close to the real planet's 95.2, but its scores aren't calibrated yet.
  8. Compass reviewed our upgrade plans: REVISE. Its three points: use STANLEY's fake-planet maker instead of building one; odd and even depths only mean something for planets that repeat; centroid checks must predict the expected shift.
  9. The STANLEY bug. Its fake-planet maker placed zero transits. Cause: before adding the transits it ran them through its search scorer, which keeps only transits already showing a dip. Before injection there's no dip, so it kept none. Our wrapper now takes the transit times straight from its orbit simulation.
  10. The realistic test. 6 fake planets, 33 crossings lasting 6.8 to 15.3 hours LIKELY. Our cleaning kept 90 to 100% of each dip. 6 Earth radii: 8 of 10 found. 8: 10 of 10. 4: none. 3 of 33 crossings were lost inside the stars' eclipses before the search even looked.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Injection and recovery is how you measure a search: add signals you know, see what comes back. It turns "we found nothing" into "nothing bigger than X crossed". Without it, a null result means nothing. Chapter 9 is all about it.

Debugging by stepping through: the STANLEY bug was found by calling its pieces one at a time. Did the orbit calculation give transit times? Yes, 13 to 29. Did they survive the next step? No. The fault sat between those two calls.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Lab 4 runs our box search on TOI-1338.
  • Lab 6 hides fake planets of several sizes and asks the search to find them.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Found: the search's floor (about 6 Earth radii), a 9% hidden loss inside eclipses, two STANLEY bugs, and a prediction confirmed.
  • Didn't: any new planet. G1 hasn't been searched yet, apart from Kepler-16.
  • Mistakes, logged: the first strict clean-up rule; a rule (C7) coded differently from how it was written; a cache that nearly wrote to C:; estimated timestamps written instead of checked ones.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why flip the light curve upside down?

A real dip becomes a bump, so the search can't find real planets in flipped data. Anything it finds there shows how often noise alone fools it.

2. 3 of 33 fake crossings fell inside eclipses. What does that mean for G1?

Even a perfect search misses about 1 crossing in 11, because we cut out the stars' eclipses before searching. Our "nothing found" results must count that loss.

docs.title: Afternoon: the Bible Overhaul begins
docs.text:
You paused the hunt so the book could catch up. Two lessons came out of the overhaul itself:

  • Labs are real runs. Every command in Labs 0 to 4 was run on your PC before it went in the book, and the "what you should see" boxes are pasted output.
  • Writing a lab caught a mistake. Our 19 October noise number for Kepler-16 (236 ppm per hour) came from a quick method that flattens away slow wobble. Measured the way our search sees the data, it's about 900 ppm; NASA's own file says 542 VERIFIED. Same data, a factor of 4 apart, depending on the method. Chapter 7 teaches why. It's logged in the mistakes register, and it probably explains the early "2 to 5 Earth radii" overstatement.
3. Why did one star's one-hour noise come out anywhere from 229 to 908 ppm?

Each method flattens the light curve differently first. The harder you flatten, the more slow wobble you remove, and the smaller the noise looks. Quote the number that matches how your search treats the data.

Later, batch 3 of the overhaul: writing Lab 8 caught a second slip. STANLEY's strongest orbit is at 96.1 days, not the 93.8 reported overnight. The search log prints the period range high to low, but the results file runs low to high. The real planet's period is 95.2 days, so the conclusion ("close") survives, but the number was wrong for half a day. Lesson: read an array's order from the data file, and check one known feature lines up. Chapter 12 and Chapter 6 are new.

Batch 4: Chapter 9 (fake planets) and Chapter 11 (pixels and neighbours), with Labs 6 and 7. Two things worth knowing: three different fake-planet tests now agree on a floor of about 6 Earth radii LIKELY; and TOI-1338's pixels show the 16 December dip on the right star, with the light's centre steady to about a thousandth of an arcsecond VERIFIED. The pixel lab uses a better error bar than our first pixel script (Compass's point): the chance spread of the same measurement at quiet times.

Batch 5: Chapter 13 (a tour of the project), Chapter 15 (our 15 mistakes, as five lessons), Lab 9 (the whole route on a G1 star of your choice), a rebuilt learning track and a reading list. Writing Lab 9 found a real problem in the G1 list: our rule "morph < 0.5" also lets in stars whose shape was never measured (morph = −1): 136 of 552 rows VERIFIED. The first star I tried was one of them, and it showed no eclipse at all. Not fixed (the hunt is paused); it's a decision for you in the decision log, explained in Chapter 1.

Batch 6, the stress test (overhaul complete): every one of the 10 lab scripts was run again from scratch and reproduced its page's "what you should see" output exactly. The built site: 40 pages, 3,743 internal links and anchors checked, 0 broken; no long dashes in visible text; no sideways scrolling on any page at phone width (375 px) or desktop width; all 11 lab and chapter pictures load; all 39 pages are in the offline cache; the "Next" links lead through all 25 chapters and labs in one line, with no loops. Your progress page now shows TOI-1338 b's recovery (19 October) and this overhaul as milestones.

docs.title: Evening: the quality-filter experiment (you approved it, I ran it)
docs.text:
In plain words

Our search throws away data that NASA flags as possibly bad. Two known crossings of TOI-1338 b fall in thrown-away data, so we couldn't see them. I tested whether keeping that data helps. The honest answer: it finds those two crossings, but it makes the search worse everywhere else, and it might add false alarms. Separately, the test turned up a surprise about which flux the search reads.

What we did and why. First I read the files (no experiment yet) and found the catch: in every piece of restored data, NASA's cleaned flux (PDCSAP) is blank; only the raw flux (SAP) exists. So "same flux, looser filter" was impossible. I wrote the plan down before running anything (experiments/quality_mask/SPEC.md): three versions, changing one thing at a time (cleaned + strict filter = our baseline; raw + strict; raw + milder). I rebuilt the baseline from scratch and checked it matched our saved results exactly. Only then did I run the other two.

The idea behind it (Chapter 8, seventh test): change one thing at a time, and decide how you'll read the result before you see it, so you can't talk yourself into the answer you like. This is called pre-registration.

What we found (one star, so treat it as a hint): - The milder filter finds both missing crossings, sectors 62 and 30, at about 12 and 10 times the noise VERIFIED. - It lowers the strength of transits elsewhere and hurts fake-planet recovery VERIFIED; false alarms: undecided VERIFIED. - Surprise: raw flux alone, with the same data points, found the published crossing in 7 sectors of 8; the cleaned flux found 4 VERIFIED. The transits are equally deep in both. What differs is the detector's noise estimate, 2 to 3 times larger in the cleaned flux in some sectors VERIFIED. We don't know why.

What we didn't find: whether any of this carries over to the G1 stars, or whether the extra false alarms are real (too few events). Nothing in the production detector or the target list was changed. All results, the spec and the code are in experiments/quality_mask/; the Compass review is in research/compass-reviews/2026-10-20-quality-mask.md.

4. Why write the plan down before running the experiment?

So the result can't be bent to fit what we hoped. Rules chosen after seeing the data are too easy to set just below the signal.

5. Raw and cleaned flux show the same transit depth, yet the detector finds the transit only in one. What differs?

The noise estimate. SNR is depth divided by noise; with a larger noise estimate the same depth gives a smaller SNR.

docs.title: 21 October 2026: a progress bar that has to prove itself
docs.text:
Field note · day 3 · about 8 min

In plain words

The home page now has a Mission readiness bar, from 0 to 100. It shows how complete and how well built our plan is. Today it reads 36. It is not the chance of finding a planet, and it can't be raised by feeling: every point needs proof, some points are counted by the program itself, and the book refuses to build if the rules are broken.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. You asked for a progress bar that updates as we learn and get closer to finding a two-sun planet. The first idea, "how close are we to a planet", can't be measured: a careful search that finds nothing is still a finished plan. So the bar measures the plan, and "Candidates found" is a separate counter.
  2. The plan is split into six stages with points that add up to 100: Know the sky (10), Detector (25), Vetting (20), Calibration (10), The search (25), Candidate to paper (10). Each stage is a list of items with a weight, so you can see exactly what is done and what is not (the Progress page).
  3. Three kinds of rule keep it honest:
    • No proof, no points. An item with credit must point to a fact in the claims register or to a file in the repo. If the proof doesn't exist, the book won't build.
    • Some points count themselves. "Stars searched out of 549" fills up by itself when the search writes targets/g1_searched.csv. "SS-0001 exists" turns on when the first real candidate is added.
    • Every change is logged. If I change a credit and forget to write a line saying why, the book won't build. The number can go down if a result is overturned.
  4. The home page status panel is now generated from the same file, so its numbers can't drift away from the truth the way my hand-typed version did.
  5. A small "Book health" line shows pages, labs and facts, and counts stale phrases. An en or em dash anywhere in the book now fails the build, because that is your rule.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A good progress measure is checkable. "We're about 40% there" is an opinion. "These 23 items, with these weights, each with proof, add up to 36" is a statement you can argue with, correct, and watch change. The weights are my first draft; they live in one file (book/progress/mission.yml) and you can change any of them.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text: Open book/progress/mission.yml. To raise a credit: change the number, add the proof, and add one line to changes with the date, the points gained and the reason. Then run .venv-docs\Scripts\python.exe book\tools\test_mission.py to check the rules, and build the book.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Today's number is 35.75, shown as 36: Know the sky 10 of 10, Detector 15 of 25, Vetting about 10 of 20, Calibration 1 of 10, the search 0 of 25 (no star of the 549 has been properly searched yet), paper 0 of 10.
  • Tested: the real rules were broken on purpose (no proof, an unlogged change, a stray dash) and each time the book refused to build with a plain message; an untouched copy built fine. The bar was checked on a phone-size screen and a desktop one, in dark and light.
  • Not done: a history graph of the number over time (a later version), and any change to the star hunt, which stays on hold until you say start.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why doesn't a bar that fills toward '100 = planet found' make sense?

Discovery isn't something we control or can measure in advance. A careful search that finds nothing is still a completed plan, so the bar measures the plan and counts candidates separately.

2. What stops someone from just typing a higher number?

Any credit needs proof (a fact or a file that exists), and every change must be logged with a reason that adds up to the total. The book refuses to build otherwise.

docs.title: 23 October 2026: rebuilding the book around a map
docs.text:
Field note · day 5 · about 8 min

In plain words

You told me the book forced labs on you, had no overview and felt disconnected, so we rebuilt it. The home page is now a map of the real sky, with three tabs, optional labs, one review page per Part and a summary at the top of every chapter. Nothing about the science changed, and the star hunt is still on hold.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. You answered 19 rounds of questions, and I wrote them into a design brief (research/BOOK-REDESIGN-BRIEF.md). You approved it and chose font B, Inter.
  2. The home page is a map of the real sky around Cygnus. The six large stars are the six Parts and the small dots around each are its chapters. Behind them are 310 real stars, the Milky Way, a chart grid, and 546 amber specks: our Kepler stars, each at its true place. (Three of our 549 have no position in the catalogue, so the caption says "546 drawn".)
  3. Three tabs, one flat list. The menu is Read, Hunt and Reference. Under Read, the fifteen chapters sit in one list with the Part names as dividers.
  4. Two ways through the same pages. The journey follows the order the project needed each idea; by topic is the textbook order. A button at the end of every chapter switches between them.
  5. Every chapter now opens the same way: a strip showing where you are, a three-line 1-minute summary, then a two-sentence plain-words box. It ends with Mark as read and a Next link that says why you might want it.
  6. Labs are optional. They moved to a "Try it yourself" page at the end of each Part, with the real output first and the commands in a fold. The chapters no longer send you to them.
  7. Questions moved too. The 48 chapter questions now live on one review page per Part ("Check yourself"), where nothing is scored or saved.
  8. Glossary words are tappable. The first time a chapter uses a term, it links to a small popup with the plain definition.
  9. A new look: the Inter font, hosted in the book so it works offline, and text colours made to a 7-to-1 contrast or better. A test now fails if the colours slip below that.
  10. Every chapter opens with a short story, in the personal voice, built only from facts already in the register (Kepler-16, TOI-1338 b and our own days), each with its label. The story of PH1 b waits until its facts are checked.
  11. Two tap-and-drag demos. In Chapter 5, two stars and a planet circle in a top-down view while a light curve is drawn beneath: set the planet's year to the real one (6.52 orbits of the stars) and it says how far apart the crossings land compared with how long each lasts. In Chapter 7, a made-up light curve with a hidden dip lets you turn up the noise, average points together and switch on a slow drift to see why averaging stops helping. In Chapter 2, the real TOI-1338 light curve from sector 98 (10-minute averages) can be dragged and zoomed, from the whole sector down to the 0.2% dip of the planet's crossing.
  12. One small diagram tops every chapter, drawn in the book's own colours (they switch with day and night): one star with three catalogue numbers, a light curve with two kinds of dip, a funnel of dips and tests, and so on.
  13. Credited NASA pictures open Parts 1 to 3 (the Kepler and K2 fields of view, and two artist's concepts of Kepler-16b, each labelled as a drawing and credited). Parts 4 to 6 have no picture yet.
  14. The story of PH1 b, the planet that volunteers found by eye, is on the new Eyes mode page. Its facts come from the paper's abstract (claim F-059, marked LIKELY because only the abstract was read).
  15. A cheat sheet for every Part: one printable page built from the chapters, with three lines per chapter, the words used and the numbers to remember. It prints as plain black on white.
  16. A Listen button on every chapter reads it aloud with your device's own voice (free, works offline, nothing is sent anywhere). It skips pictures, code, tables and the source list, highlights what it is saying, and Pause remembers the place.
  17. Eyes mode, practice version. You see a day and a half of the real TOI-1338 light curve with nothing marked and answer Dip, No dip, Odd or Not sure; then the hidden thing is outlined. Sittings are 5, 20, 50 or 100 light curves. The stretches contain fake dips we hid, glitches, real eclipses and the real planet crossing, so the answer is always known. The real stars of the hunt are not connected: the hunt stays on hold until you say start.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text: A map is a promise about where things are. To draw part of the sky on a flat page you need each star's position (right ascension and declination, like longitude and latitude on the sky) and a rule for flattening a sphere. We used a gnomonic projection, which keeps straight lines straight and distorts only a little over a patch this size. Brightness becomes dot size: a smaller magnitude number means a brighter star, so it gets a bigger dot. Colour comes from the star's spectral type. That is why the map is real: change the catalogue and the picture changes.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text: Open book/data/path.yml: it lists the Parts, the fifteen chapters, their summaries and the journey order. Edit a line, then run .venv-docs\Scripts\python.exe -m mkdocs build --strict inside book, and the map, the strips and the Next links all follow. To redraw the sky from fresh catalogues, book/tools/make_sky.py (needs the internet) rewrites book/data/sky.json.

docs.title: What we found, and what we didn't
docs.text:
• Tested: the strict build passes; a link checker followed every link and anchor on all 61 built pages; the colour test passes; the home page does not scroll sideways at phone width; the glossary popup, Mark as read and the reading-order switch all worked in the browser.
  • Not done yet: eyes mode on the hunt's real stars (waits for your start), a recorded voice instead of the device voice (a better-sounding tool, your call), and pictures for Parts 4 to 6. They are the next phases in the brief.
  • Not tested: the Listen button was tested with a stand-in voice in a browser with no sound, so how it sounds on your phone is unchecked. You have not read it yet. The real test is your 15 minutes: tell me where you got lost and that goes to the top of the fix list.

docs.title: Later the same night: breaking it on purpose
docs.text:
After the build I tried to break the book, which is where the real lessons were.

  • A tool crashed on our map. The theme rewrites every link on a page when you move between pages, and that code throws an error on links inside an SVG picture, because an SVG link's address is read-only. A screenshot would never show it; a browser test that listens for errors did. The map's links now use the older xlink:href form, and the error is gone.
  • Sizes need a ruler, not an eye. A script measured every tappable thing at phone width. The map's dots were about 15 pixels wide, too small for a thumb, and several links were short. They are now at least 24 pixels (the map) or 44 (everything else), and the check runs before every publish.
  • Numbers must agree on a page. Building the explorer from the real data showed that Chapter 2 gave the primary eclipse as 5.1% and the secondary as 0.4%, while our measured values (claim F-046) are about 6% at the bottom (5.7% typical) and 0.3%. The table now uses the measured values with their label.
  • Facts need their labels even in summaries. The new summaries repeated numbers (14 planets, one in four candidates) without the little VERIFIED chips. They have them now.
  • A rule only counts if you have seen it refuse. Ten deliberately broken copies (a missing chapter, a sidebar that disagrees with the page order, a story that is too long) are each refused by book/tools/test_shape.py. A page nobody links to, a stray dash and a colour that fails 7-to-1 are also caught.

Idea: test the failure, not the happy path. A check you have never seen fail is a hope, not a check.

You could try it: in book/data/path.yml, change one chapter's part and run the build. It stops with a plain message instead of publishing a book whose map and menu disagree.

docs.title: Afternoon: an outside review finds two silent bugs
docs.text:
A separate Claude, with web access and a copy of our code, answered our research brief. Everything went through Compass first: I re-ran each bug here with my own scripts, recounted its numbers from our target files and looked up all 20 of its papers in ADS. All 20 were real (Gemini's answer had 7 of 12 wrong). Full review: research/compass-reviews/2026-10-23-deep-review.md.

  • Bug 1: the detector was blind on 30-minute data. It averages the light into 10-minute bins and ignores any box less than 80% full. With one point every 30 minutes only a third of the bins have data, so every box is ignored. I hid an obvious dip (signal 23 times the noise) in fake data: found at 2, 3.3 and 10-minute spacing, nothing at 30. TESS took 30-minute pictures until 2020, and Kepler's own light curves are 30-minute, so the planned Kepler test would have failed for no real reason.
  • Bug 2: old QLP files used the wrong column. Before sector 56, QLP's flattened column has a different name (kspsap_flux), and the loader picked it. It is the same flattening we had already caught shrinking a 6-hour dip by about 70%. Our one QLP test happened to use sector 98, which has the good column, so it passed.
  • Together they touch about half of the planned QLP data. Nothing has been searched yet, so no result is wrong, but those stars would have looked quiet.
  • The odds moved up a little, to about 20% (range 5 to 45%). The outside estimate was 21 to 39%, but it used the noise of TOI-1338, a quiet star outside our list. Kepler-16, the one star of ours we have measured, is about twice as noisy. With that noise the same sum gives about 17%.
  • Timing matters: TESS looks at the Kepler field again in July and August 2027. A candidate published with a predicted date before then can be checked by TESS itself.

docs.title: Evening: the fixes, and the first look at our own stars' noise
docs.text:
You said to apply the changes and make sure nothing breaks, so the order was: tests first, then fixes, then proof.

  • Tests that fail first. A new check hides a dip at five spacings (2, 3.3, 10, 29.4 and 30 minutes) and reads our real QLP and SPOC files. On the old code it failed at 29.4 minutes; on the new code all of it passes.
  • The fixes. The detector now averages into bins as wide as the data's own spacing when that is slower than 10 minutes. Old QLP sectors use the raw flux (it keeps the dip's depth). A file whose cleaned column is empty now falls back to the raw one instead of returning nothing.
  • Nothing else broke. The old and new detector both ran on all 51 light curves we have: 50 gave exactly the same results, and the one that changed is the old QLP file, as intended.
  • The audit, tried on 7 of our stars. In every sector it hides one standard dip and checks that it comes back: it always did where the noise allowed, and never where it did not. It also measures how much worse than ideal the noise is. The middle value is 1.76 times the ideal, and Kepler-16 is about 1.9, not the 2.8 I quoted this afternoon: that number came from a different way of measuring. So the odds lean a little up, but these 7 stars are brighter than most of ours, so I keep about 20% until all 549 are measured.
  • One early letdown, later corrected: on the one Kepler-16 sector I tried, the old QLP raw flux was about six times noisier than SPOC's. I took that as typical. When all 549 stars were measured (below), the real figure is about 1.2 times.

docs.title: Night: the Kepler test
docs.text: With the 30-minute bug fixed, the detector could finally read the original Kepler data. We downloaded four years of it for Kepler-16, 34 and 35 (52 files, 21 MB). No list of the exact transit times could be opened, so I found the transits a different way first, and checked each one by eye: 7 for Kepler-16, 7 for Kepler-34 and 4 for Kepler-35. Then the real detector ran blind. It found all 18, in both kinds of flux, at 13 to 320 times the noise. Most of its extra events sat at the edges of Kepler's monthly pauses, which our rules already flag for a person. One extra dip happened at the same moment on two different stars, which can only be the spacecraft. The honest limit: the transits I could see by eye are the easy ones, so this is not yet a fair race against Davies et al., who counted 9 for Kepler-34 and 7 for Kepler-35.

docs.title: Late night: you said go, in stages
docs.text:
You approved the first two stages of the hunt: preparation, then measuring all 549 stars. Searching them is not approved yet, and nothing is searched in these stages.

  • Three small tools were added and tested. (1) Every eclipse period of a star is now masked, not only the one that passed our cut. Two stars have a second one; with it left unmasked a test star gave 175 false events, and with it masked, none. (2) An event that also appears upside down is now only flagged in the hunt, not deleted, until we have measured what that deletion loses. (3) A same-moment filter: if three or more other stars on the same camera show an event within 2.4 hours of each other, the cause is the spacecraft, so all of them are flagged for a person. My first rule (two other stars) flagged 4% of purely random events by chance, so I tightened it; chance now flags under 0.5%.
  • The download started: every light curve of every one of the 549 stars, about 8,400 files and 6 GB, saved on D: and logged one star at a time. It takes about two hours because NASA's archive answers slowly, not because of the file size.

docs.title: Then: all 549 stars measured
docs.text:
The download finished (549 stars, 8,100 files, 5.4 GB) and the audit ran on every file. It did not search anything: in each star-sector it hides one standard dip, checks that it comes back, and records the noise. Nothing failed.

  • Our coverage table was wrong in one place. It listed 1,629 SPOC 2-minute star-sectors; the real number is 1,304. The extra 325 were multi-sector summary entries, not light curves. The star counts in the book were right.
  • The honest picture of what we can see. In a single 6.5-hour crossing, the smallest planet we could detect is below 6 Earth radii in only 196 of 5,064 star-sectors, and below 15 in 1,944. For 143 stars the best sector reaches 10 Earth radii; for 269, 15. For 239 stars (43%) no sector gets below 15, bigger than every known planet around two stars. The hidden test dip came back in 73% of sectors of stars brighter than magnitude 11, but only 8% at magnitude 12 to 13 and 1% beyond. Faint stars are close to blind.
  • The noise is about 2.5 times worse than ideal (median, from 1.7 to 4.0), not the 1.76 from the first seven stars, which were brighter than most. That is the number that decides our odds.
  • The products are closer than I feared. TESS-SPOC is as quiet as SPOC (1.05 times). Old QLP raw flux is about 1.2 times, newer QLP about 1.4 times. A star that only has QLP is not hopeless.
  • Borrowing the good stretches from neighbouring stars works: across 1,298 checks it kept 87% of each star's own good time and added almost no bad time.
  • False alarms are heavily clustered. Upside-down, the detector makes 0.17 fake events per star-sector, 869 in all, and 41% of them fall at moments when three or more other stars also show one: the spacecraft, not the stars. Our new filter flags those. Even so, about 520 fakes would be left for a person at our current bar. At a much higher bar of 12 there would still be about 110. So the next stage has to test more automatic checks, such as the same dip appearing in two independent data products.
  • The odds hardly moved: with each star's own noise, the chance of at least one real candidate comes out between 15% and 21%. I now say about 18% (range 5 to 40%).

Idea: measure the whole population before you trust a sample. Seven bright stars said the noise was 1.76 times ideal; all 549 said 2.5.

Idea: a filter must be tested against pure chance too. A rule that flags the real thing is not enough if it also flags 4% of the noise.

Idea: a filter that silently returns nothing looks exactly like a quiet star. Every way the data can come in (each product, spacing and era) needs a test that hides a known dip and fails loudly if it does not come back.

You could try it: research/deep-review-2026-10-23/our-checks/verify_b1_b2.py prints the four spacings and which column the loader picks for each QLP file we have.

docs.title: Midnight: the first real search, machine only
docs.text:
You approved a trial on 50 stars: the 5 known planet hosts as controls and 45 others spread by brightness. You asked for the machine-only version first. I will only ask you to look with your own eyes once you have practised Eyes mode and can pass a test on it.

Nothing real is published from this run: the stars and times of every event stay on this computer, and only counts appear here.

  • There are fewer real dips than fake ones. Per star-sector the search finds 0.08 real events and 0.18 upside-down events. So the upside-down count over-estimates false alarms (flares and scattered light make more bumps than dips), and nothing in this sample shows an overall excess of real dips.
  • Two thirds of the events sit within half a day of a data gap or a thruster firing. They are flagged for lower priority, not deleted, because a real planet can sit there: two of the four TOI-1338 b crossings did.
  • The automatic checks shrink the list a lot. Of 36 real events at our bar, 12 are left after the gap and thruster flags, 7 after removing moments when other stars also dip and events that also appear upside-down, and 4 after removing events that sit on the star's own eclipse.
  • A second data product agrees with a real dip about 9 times in 10 (91%, for strong fake dips we hid in both), but with only about half the false alarms (49%). So it removes about half the false alarms and costs about 9% of strong dips. Weak dips would lose more; we have not measured that.
  • The eclipse-phase check caught two of five leads sitting on the star's own eclipse, which the automatic mask had missed on noisy, variable stars. It removes about the same share of fake events (19%) as real ones (17%), so it is a safety net, not a magic filter.
  • The controls behaved. On the five known hosts no real planet crossing is expected. Two events passed the flags: one a junk ramp in old QLP flux, one on Kepler-453 with the known planet's depth but a quarter of its length, sitting 0.1 days from where the binary's second eclipse should be. Most likely the binary, not the planet.
  • Projected to all 549 stars: about 60 first-tier events for a person to look at (uncertain by about a factor of two), plus a lower tier of about 350 flagged ones.
  • Three leads survived every check. One is weak. Two look clean but come from stars that only have QLP data, so a second product cannot confirm them. They are leads, not candidates: they need a look at the pixels and the neighbours, and nothing is announced.

Idea: a control is a star where you already know the answer. Any event there is a false alarm until it is proved otherwise.

Idea: a check that removes the same share of real and fake events is a safety net, not a filter. Know which one you are holding.

You could try: open research/stage2-2026-10-23/aggregate.txt and compare the real and upside-down columns at each bar.

docs.title: The small hours: Eyes mode now keeps your scores
docs.text:
You told me the practice mode forgot your score, and that I should have built the saving before. You were right: I made it a practice game with saving switched off, and I never asked whether the scores mattered. They did, and your first practice rounds are gone.

  • Every answer is saved on your device the moment you give it. A round you leave half done is kept and marked abandoned. Nothing about an old answer can be edited: the save code only accepts the next unanswered question.
  • After every answer a big banner says the truth: THIS WAS: A DIP, or THIS WAS: NOT A DIP, what it was (a hidden planet, a quiet stretch, an eclipse, a spike, a jump), and whether you were right. If you said No dip to an eclipse, it says you were right that it is not a dip but that it was an eclipse.
  • You can look back through the round, read only. You see the curve and what you answered. In the test the truth stays hidden until the end.
  • My results lists every round: right, wrong, not sure, dips found, false alarms. (I first added a "Copy my results" button as a fallback. You hated it, rightly: you should never have to hand me your own scores. It is gone; the cloud copy will do it by itself.)
  • The official test is 30 curves (10 clear dips, 4 faint, 8 quiet, 8 odd) with no answers until the end. The pass line you chose: at least 85% of clear dips and at most 1 in 10 quiet curves called a dip, over at least 60 curves, in 2 or more rounds, on 2 or more days. Faint dips are reported but are not in the line.
  • Not done yet: the cloud copy. Until it is set up, results live on the device you used, so add the book to your phone's Home Screen.
  • Built to be reused: the Eyes engine takes its light curves from a swappable source. The real candidates of the hunt will get their own tab, using this same engine, once Claude agrees your results are good enough.
  • Tested: 17 checks of the scoring and saving logic and 33 checks in a real browser (answering, looking back, the test, an abandoned round, a reload, phone layout). I also broke the code on purpose five ways in the logic and three ways in the browser, and each break was caught. My first browser break-test was invalid (a text-encoding slip of mine mangled the arrow buttons) and it only showed up because I re-ran the unbroken version.

Idea: before you build a tool, ask what it must remember. A practice tool that forgets is fine until the day you want to know how you are doing.

Idea: a test that has never failed has not been tested. Break the thing on purpose and watch the test notice, then re-run the unbroken version to be sure the test, not your break, is what failed.

docs.title: Morning: your scores now reach the cloud by themselves
docs.text:
You set up Firebase, and the cloud backup is built. You never copy or send anything.

  • How it works: the moment you finish a round, or leave one half done, the book sends it to a private cloud copy (your Firebase project). If you are offline, the round waits on your phone and goes out the moment the internet is back. The line under the results says what is happening, from "sending your round" to "all 3 finished rounds are safe in the cloud, and Claude can read them".
  • No double copies: each round has its own unique name, and the cloud refuses a second copy with the same name, so a send that was interrupted can be tried again safely.
  • What Claude does: a reader signs in with a key only your computer holds, pulls every round, scores it with the same code the book uses, and writes the practice and test rounds into the repo as the permanent record. A daily job does this each morning, and Claude can do it any time you say "look at my eye test scores".
  • Your rules, tested from the outside: I tried a good write (accepted), a repeat (refused as already there), nine kinds of junk (all refused), and reading, changing and deleting with the public key (all refused). Only the reader's key can read.
  • Proof it works: a real browser played a round, it reached your real Firebase, and I compared it field by field with what the browser had saved: all 5 answers, the totals and the timing were identical. Then I deleted the test round.
  • Tested: 20 checks of the scoring logic, 11 of the sender (offline, retries, a busy server, no duplicates), 14 in a real browser against a pretend Firestore (online, offline, a server error, an abandoned round), 34 on the Eyes screen. Each family was broken on purpose to prove it can fail. One of the first break-tests did not catch a removed "internet is back" listener, because a background check rescued the round, so I slowed that check down and made the test demand delivery within 10 seconds.
  • Still not done: the Training record page and the real-candidate page (waiting for your go), and a test on your real iPhone: I can only test in a computer browser, so tell me if anything looks off on the phone.

Idea: the test of a safety net is whether it holds when you cut the first rope. If a backup path can rescue a failure, a test that only checks "it arrived in the end" cannot tell which path did the work.

docs.title: Night: an outside brief on how to show you the dots, and what it taught us about our own practice
docs.text:
Another Claude, with web access, wrote a research brief on how a page should present a candidate dip to a beginner and to an AI without one anchoring the other. I did not build from it. I checked it first (our Compass review), and I read the original papers for its key claims.

  • What held up: hiding the star's name until after the answer, hidden fake dips with known answers, an equal-sized "unclear" button, no planet-shaped model drawn on the data before both answers are in, and scoring "can you see dips" separately from "do you say planet too easily". I read the Planet Hunters TESS and Space Warps papers and the TESS vetting paper: the quoted rates (30% fake dips at the start, falling to 1%, or never below 10% in Space Warps) and the "undecided" option are really there. The medical result that a wrong AI hint can drag even experts down to about 45% accuracy is reported consistently, but I only read news coverage of it, so I call it likely, not proven.
  • What would have been a mistake: the lineup test. The idea is to hide the real dip among a few empty stretches and see if you can pick it out. I tried it in a simulation of pure noise with no planet at all. If the empty stretches are random, a perfect observer still picks "the dip" 84% of the time, because the dip was chosen as the biggest wiggle of the whole sector and a random stretch is not. If the empty stretches are the biggest wiggle found by the same search on other noise, the observer drops to 20%, which is pure chance, as it should be. The comparison is only fair when both sides were picked the same way.
  • What it showed about our own practice: your "quiet" practice curves are random stretches. On real data you will only ever see the machine's best-looking wiggle in each sector. So your false-alarm score on easy quiet curves understates how often you would be fooled for real. The fix is a new kind of practice card, "noise at its best", built from the detector's top event on upside-down or noise-only data.
  • Our pass line, measured: I simulated readers of known skill. Someone who truly finds 75% of dips and false-alarms 12% of the time meets the line in the first two rounds about 9% of the time; someone at 90% and 8% meets it only 55% of the time. So the line is a fair gate but a noisy one, and that is why I judge the numbers and do not just read the line.
  • What it changes: the current Eyes practice teaches shapes, but it is a clean 36 hour cutout of one star. The real page will show a whole sector, a zoom, where the dip falls in the stars' own eclipse cycle and a second data product, on many stars with different noise. A new layout needs its own readiness test, so a rehearsal with hidden fakes in the real layout is now required before any real lead, not optional.
