  • Nothing was built. This was a review. The full verdict is in research/compass-reviews/2026-10-24-vetting-page-research.md.

Idea: a test is only fair if the thing you check and the thing you compare it with were chosen the same way. Picking the best-looking stretch of the data and comparing it with an ordinary stretch proves nothing.

Idea: before you ask whether you are good at spotting something, ask whether your practice material is as hard as the real material. Easy practice gives a flattering score.

You could try: open research/vetting-page-research-2026-10-23/our_checks.py and change the lineup simulation so the empty stretches are random again; watch the 20% turn into 84%.

docs.title: Night: your first official test, 11 rounds in 25 minutes
docs.text:
You did 11 official test rounds and one practice round in about 25 minutes, and the cloud copy arrived by itself. I read them without you sending anything.

  • The numbers: clear dips found 102 of 110 (93%, 95% range 86% to 96%). Faintest dips 37 of 44 (84%). Quiet curves called a dip 10 of 88 (11%). Eclipses, spikes and jumps named correctly 84 of 88 (95%).
  • The learning curve is the real story. In the first 6 rounds you called 10 of 48 quiet curves a dip (21%). In the last 5 rounds it was 0 of 40, and 50 of 50 clear dips found. Your d-prime (how well you tell dips from not-dips, where 0 is guessing and about 3 is excellent) went from 2.1 to 3.7, and your criterion stayed near 0, so you are not just saying "dip" more or less often.
  • Where the early misses were: 9 of the first 12 misses were deep, long fake dips (4,000 ppm, 6 to 8 hours) that you called "odd", taking them for eclipses. By round 4 that mistake was gone.
  • Your wrong answers were slower (median 2.2 s against 1.1 s for right ones). Hesitating on the ones you get wrong is a good sign.
  • What the numbers cannot say: the fake dips come from one generator on one star, as clean boxes of three fixed depths. Real dips have soft edges, and the real TOI-1338 b card was the same transit every round, so from round 5 you answered it in under a second. You also never pressed "Not sure" in 330 curves and never looked back. On real data "not sure" will often be the honest answer, so that needs practice.
  • The day rule stays, but it is small. The pass line asks for 2 different days, not 5. The rounds you did count as one day, because they all fell on the same calendar date. Why not let volume replace the second day: within one sitting you went from 21% false alarms to 0%, which shows how fast you learn, and also that one sitting cannot separate "learned the trick in the last 20 minutes" from "keeps it tomorrow". One cold round on another date answers that, and it takes about a minute.

Idea: a score that climbs steeply inside one session is good news about the learner and bad news about the test. Ask what changed between the first round and the last.

Idea: speed can mean skill or it can mean a memorised look. The way to tell them apart is to change the look and see whether the speed survives.

docs.title: Night: the hard test, built the same night you asked
docs.text:
You said 30 out of 30 had become boring, so step two of the ladder is built and live: Hard practice (answers after every curve) and Take the HARD test (30 curves, no answers until the end), with its own line.

  • The line, fixed before you played it: at least 80% of the clear fake planets found, and at most 20% of the hard-noise cards called a dip, over at least 4 hard rounds, 120 curves and 2 different days. On a clear fake planet Not sure counts as a miss. On hard noise it is free.
  • Hard noise is not random any more. Each "nothing hidden" card is the best-looking dip found in a whole fresh sector of noise, because that is what the hunt will hand you. I made the noise by reshuffling 6 hour pieces of this star's own noise.
  • The fake planets go down to the edge. Strength 10 to 16 for the clear ones, 5 to 8.5 for the near-limit ones (the hunt keeps 7 and above), with sloping sides instead of boxes.
  • New odd things: a dip that ends where a gap in the data begins (the thruster-firing artifact), a jump down that never recovers, and subtler spikes. Eclipses are real eclipses of this star. The old memorised planet card is gone.
  • How hard it really is: for a perfect box-shaped filter, the hard-noise cards have a median strength of 6.1 and 30% reach 7 or above. The clear fakes beat every noise card. The near-limit fakes at 5 to 6.5 cannot be told from ordinary hard noise, so there Not sure is the right answer, not a dodge.
  • The test caught my first version. I made the noise from the star's own leftovers, and the checks said the "noise" had a median strength of 19. The star's data holds real glitches, and reshuffling them put a huge dip in every card. The fix was to leave out any piece that already holds an obvious dip or bump. Without a check that measured the cards, I would have shipped a test full of hidden eclipses-by-accident.
  • Tested: 15 checks of the cards and scoring, a browser run of a whole hard test and a hard practice round, and I broke the code on purpose 10 ways (unselected noise, an event always in the middle, weaker fakes, a missing gap, wrong Not sure scoring, the two lines mixing, a moved line); every break was caught.
  • Looking at the live page caught a second flaw. In my first version, any card with a gap in the data was the "dip at a gap" card, so a gap alone gave the answer away. Now about 4 in 10 of the other cards carry a gap too, kept well away from the event, so only a dip that touches a gap counts. Two more deliberate breaks of that rule were caught.
  • Still one star. All of this uses TOI-1338's sector 98. The rehearsal in step three uses many stars.

Idea: build a thing that makes fake data, then measure the fake data. If you never check that your fake noise behaves like noise, your whole test rests on a guess.

Idea: fix the pass mark before anyone plays. A line chosen after the scores are in is not a line.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why do bigger dots mean brighter stars on the map?

Magnitude is backwards: a smaller number is brighter. The map turns that into a dot size, so the brightest stars (like Deneb) are drawn largest.

2. Why does the caption say 546 drawn, not 549?

Three of our stars have no sky position in the Villanova Kepler catalogue, and we only draw what we can place. The book says so rather than rounding up.

3. Why did a dip that was obvious at 10-minute spacing vanish at 30-minute spacing?

The detector only trusted boxes that were at least 80% full of 10-minute bins. At 30-minute spacing two bins in three are empty, so no box ever qualified and the search returned nothing, with no error.

4. Seven stars said the noise was 1.76 times ideal; all 549 said about 2.5. Why trust the second number?

The first seven were brighter than most and had the best data. The 549 are the whole list, including faint stars where noise is worse. A sample only describes the population it was drawn from.

5. Why do we flag events near data gaps instead of deleting them?

Because a real planet can sit there. Two of the four TOI-1338 b crossings we re-found were within half a day of a gap or a thruster firing. Flagged events go to a lower-priority list for a person to check later.

6. The eclipse-phase check removes 17% of real events and 19% of fake ones. What kind of check is that?

A safety net, not a filter. It does not separate real from fake (the shares are about equal); it just catches a specific mistake, an eclipse the mask missed, at the price of ignoring the stretches near eclipses.

7. Why can the look-back button never change an answer?

The saving code only accepts the next unanswered question of a round that is still open. An old answer is never written again, and the tests try to change one and check that it fails.

docs.title: 24 October 2026: feedback that is measured, not copied
docs.text:
Field note · day 6 · about 9 min

In plain words

You said the comments under each card felt copy-pasted. They were: a few hand-written sentences per kind of noise. Now every card gets three lines worked out from its own dots, in practice and in the review after a test. Before building that, we found that our own practice cards gave their answer away in a way you could learn without learning the sky, and fixed most of it.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. A review before any building. Claude AI wrote a report and a working prototype for the feedback lines. I ran it through Compass (my review step), tested it on our cards and on your exact hard-practice cards, and the verdict was revise: good idea, five things to fix first. Nothing was built until you chose to.
  2. One strength score everywhere. The card banner and the new lines were measuring "strength" in two different ways, so one of your hard-noise cards read 7.3 in one place and 10.2 in the other. I ported the hunt's own scoring (the box_scores function in the detector) to the page, and a test feeds the same numbers to the Python and to the page and demands the same answers.
  3. The cards stopped giving themselves away (mostly). On the first version the quiet "best dip of a sector" was short (about 3 hours at its best box) while the fake planets were about 6.5 hours, so a quiet card could be told from a fake by its length alone. Now half of the quiet cards are chosen to be as long as a fake planet, the fakes run from 3 to 12 hours, and the test measures how much each feature separates the two kinds.
  4. Three lines, worked out from the dots. Each is 36 to 44 words. Line 1 is a measurement ("the dip ends only 1 hour before a hole in the data"), line 2 says what that usually means, line 3 says what it was and what to check next time. About 20 kinds of fact are measured, each with several wordings that rotate.
  5. The lead lesson never looks at the hidden answer. The answer only decides the last line. Real work will not have an answer to look up, so the practice has to learn to use the dots.
  6. The strength of every card you answer is now saved with your answer. That is the data for a line that shows your own habit, for example how often you said Dip on cards under 7.
  7. Three extras for your practice. After you answer, the plot shows a dashed line (how deep a dip must be here to score 7) and a solid line (how deep the best stretch really is). My results has a new table, Your habit by strength: how often you said Dip at each strength, where you start saying Dip more than half the time, your d-prime and your criterion. And in practice a curve you got wrong comes back 3 to 5 curves later (the sitting keeps the same curves; tests are never reordered).
  8. Twin drill. In Hard mode, two curves with the same noise, one with a faint planet and one without. You pick which. It is never saved and counts towards nothing, because it is practice, not evidence. The cards are built from one seed with and without the planet, and a test checks that outside the planet the two curves are identical.
  9. Broken on purpose 18 ways, every break caught. That includes a lead that peeks at the answer, "missed" said about a false alarm, wrong lengths, a changed scale, a quiet card always placed in the same spot, a criterion with the wrong sign and a miss that comes back too soon.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (a leak): if a feature of your practice material predicts the answer but has nothing to do with the sky, you can learn the feature and feel clever. The check is a number between 0 and 1 called AUC: 0.5 means the feature tells the two kinds apart no better than a coin, 1 means it always does. In the first version, length separated faint fake planets from quiet cards at 0.84. Now it is 0.66. Position of the event (0.47), holes in the data (0.46) and how strong the runner-up wiggle is (0.40) are near a coin.

Idea (honest leftovers): not all of that is a flaw. Noise peaks really are shorter than planet dips, so some separation by length is true to the sky. And strength now separates them at 0.71 (it was 0.50 only because the old cards were matched through the length leak). The lines say this plainly instead of hiding it.

Idea (blind lead): a text that picks its lesson by looking at the hidden answer is just reading the answer back to you. The lead is chosen from measurements only. I measured how often the answer-aware choice would have led differently: 16% of practice cards.

Idea (near miss): a card that comes close to a known artifact pattern without crossing its test line is called not classified, never plain noise. On ordinary cards this fires about 3 times in 100. In real mode, 0.8% of artifact cards ended up with "pure noise" as the lead.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Run node book/tools/test_eyes_feedback.mjs and read the 16 checks. Change a lesson's test in book/docs/assets/eyes-feedback.js and see which check fails.
  • Run node book/tools/test_eyes_mutations.mjs: it breaks the code 18 ways and prints "caught" for each. A test that still passes on broken code is not testing anything.
  • Open research/compass-reviews/2026-10-24-feedback-engine.md to see the five fixes and the numbers behind them.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found: the pre-hole sag is caught on 95% of fake gap dips and on 0 of 640 ordinary cards. A brightening is caught on 94% of spikes (0.2% false), eclipses on 100%, level jumps on 72% (1.1% false). Your four missed gap dips would now have read, for example: "In the 2 hours before the hole at 10.5 hours, light sags by 1,100 ppm. A sag that ends exactly where data stops is the classic thruster firing fake."
  • Variety: over 60 hard-noise cards in one sitting there are 28 to 38 different second lines (the prototype gave 20), with the numbers masked. You will still meet a repeat now and then.
  • Faint fakes and hard noise still overlap. Hard noise scores about 4.5 in the middle and about 1 in 6 cards reaches 7. The near-limit fakes measure 4 to 9 once the noise is added. So Not sure stays a fair answer on the faintest ones.
  • Not found out: the hunt's scale here comes from this star's reshuffled noise, which is nearly white beyond a few hours. The real sector is lumpier, so long boxes would score lower on real data than here. The easy sitting's windows are raw, not flattened as the hunt flattens them, so its numbers are a little rougher. And none of this has been tried on a real iPhone yet.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why must the lead lesson not look at the hidden answer?

Because in real work there is no hidden answer. A practice text that quotes the answer teaches you to read the answer, not the dots.

2. What does an AUC of 0.5 mean for a feature like position?

It tells the two kinds of card apart no better than a coin toss, so learning it teaches you nothing about the generator.

3. Why is a card that nearly matches an artifact never called plain noise?

A near miss means something is there that the tests did not explain. Calling it plain noise would reassure you wrongly, so it is called not classified.

docs.title: 27 October 2026: measure the advice before you take it
docs.text:
Field note · day 9 · about 8 min

In plain words

Since the last note, three pieces of outside advice came in: a design brief, a font report and our own plan for the learning path. We did not build any of them on trust. We measured them first, and each time something turned up that reading alone would have missed. We also added a plain score line to Eyes mode and two pages for professional astronomers.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. The design brief was checked with a calculator. Another AI wrote a brief for a new look. I ran it through Compass (my review step). Its "muted brass" text colour measured 2.9 to 1 against our rule of 7 to 1. The brief asked for 60 to 70 characters per line, but a phone at 375 pixels fits only about 35 to 42. The revised brief then failed its own colour rule on two surfaces (2.94 and 2.69 against a minimum of 3). A script found that, not reading.
  2. The font report was checked against the font files. You do not like the current look, so we asked another AI which fonts would suit the book. Its answer was sensible, but it never said which characters each font has. I read the character list inside the four font files the book serves today. All four lack σ, μ, λ, Δ, θ, ≈, ≥, ≤ and →. The book uses σ 38 times, ≈ 28 times and μ 11 times, so on your phone those characters come from the phone's own font, not from Inter. That may be part of why the type feels off.
  3. A font test you can read on your phone. A private page shows a real paragraph of this book in five font pairings, night or day, and checks which symbols each font has. Nothing in the book changes until you choose.
  4. The learning path was reviewed, you said yes, and it is built. The book had three reading orders: chapter numbers, the order the project needed them, and the seven learning levels. Four chapters (3, 13, 14, 15) belonged to no level at all. Now the levels are the one path, starting with the first thing to learn and building up. Chapter 3 joined Level 0, chapters 13 to 15 became a last step after Level 6, and the Journey and By topic buttons are gone. The old journey list is now the story page "How the project unfolded". Chapter numbers stay as permanent labels, so the path reads 1, 2, 3, then 7, 8, then 4, 5, 6. Each chapter shows your level and step, and the next link leads to the next level.
  5. Eyes mode now says your score first. After every practice or test, the top of the finish screen says "You got N of 30 right", then how many were wrong and Not sure, and how often you picked each answer. You no longer open My results to find it.

  6. Two pages for professional readers. For astronomers says in one page what is solid and what is not, and Prior work lists the published searches we know and how deeply we have read each. Both say plainly that we have found no planet.

  7. The redesign is a plan you can look at before anything is built. A private page shows what changes and how, with a phone chapter, a PC chapter and a PC Eyes screen drawn from the real Chapter 2 text, two real claims and a real light curve. Nothing in the live book changed, and nothing is built until you approve it.

  8. The plan was revised after your feedback, and a font was measured for it. You asked for Atkinson against Literata, a quieter note margin and an Eyes layout that scrolls naturally. The new private page has seven boards. We also tested which font should draw σ, ≈ and √. Inter, my first idea, has Greek but not the maths signs. A cut of Noto Sans Math is 1.9 KB and covers everything the book uses, with one more glyph (✗) in a 0.9 KB file. You picked Atkinson and left the other choices to us.

  9. The next hunt stage is prepared but not run. Stage 3 would search all 549 stars. Before it, we wrapped the Stage 2 search so its results go to a folder named after the settings, added the eclipse-phase check to every event, labelled the 237 stars that have only one light curve, and checked the eclipse shape of the 136 stars whose shape was never measured. No star was searched and the settings are not frozen.
  10. Your Eyes results were read, and the page that shows them was found cluttered. Over 25 finished rounds (665 curves; every dip is a fake hidden in real noise, and no real candidate has been shown yet), you found 93% of the clear dips in the standard test, and in the last five rounds you called none of 40 quiet curves a dip. Your misses come in three kinds: faint dips under strength 6.5 (you found 14 of 30), jumps and dips at a gap taken for a dip (12 of 82), and early on, deep dips called "odd" (9 times in the first five rounds, never after). You said the stats are hard to find, and the code shows why: after a hard test the same sentences are printed two or three times. The redesign plan now says one fact in one place, verdict first.
  11. The real redesign started, in two steps. You said start, so the book now uses Atkinson Hyperlegible Next for text and headings, IBM Plex Sans for menus and labels, and two tiny symbol files for σ, μ, Δ, ≈, √, ≥ and 13 other maths and star signs, so every phone draws them the same way. A new test checks that all 31 special characters in the book are drawn by a font the book carries. On a PC window 1120 pixels or wider, a chapter now has a left rail (where you are, the 7-level track and the 15 chapters as two labelled lists), a 540-pixel reading column and a quiet margin that opens only the evidence or glossary note nearest the middle of the screen. A new browser test checks all of that at seven window widths. We also removed two sentences that the hard-test finish screen printed twice. The Eyes layout for PC came next (item 13); the final look pass is not built yet.
  12. The design was reviewed by another AI, and the review changed the results screen. I drew a results screen that said "you catch clear fake planets every time and you rarely cry wolf". The review pointed out that your standard test missed 8 of 110 clear dips and called 10 of 88 quiet curves a dip, 11.4%, above the 10% limit. So the screen now says what the numbers say: "You found 92.7% of the clear dips. False alarms on quiet curves are above the limit of 10%." Every measure shows its count, its target and a bar with the target marked. The 95% confidence interval is named in full and explained once, and a practice result is never called a pass. The weakest spot is worded as a pattern to check, not a proven cause. The older lists sit behind "All the numbers". Margin notes also got a rule: a note that cannot sit within 120 pixels of what it explains is left out of the margin, and the chip in the text still works.
  13. Eyes mode got its PC layout. On a window 1220 pixels or wider, the curve sits on the left with the four answer buttons in one row under it and Next under them, and what the numbers say sits on the right. On a 1366 by 650 screen you now see the curve, the feedback and Next at once. The contents list on the right of this page is hidden to make room. The curve's height follows its own shape (0.55 of its width, never under 170 or over 340 pixels), not a share of the window. The Next slot is reserved from the start, so nothing jumps when the feedback appears; on narrower screens it is pinned to the bottom of the window only once there is a Next to press. After Next, the keyboard focus moves to the first answer instead of vanishing. Scoring, saving and the cloud are untouched. A new browser test checks five window sizes (a phone, a zoomed PC, 1024 by 768, 1366 by 650, 1440 by 900): no overlap, every button at least 44 pixels, the answers in one row where there is room, the focus kept.
  14. The real search of all 549 stars ran. You said start, so the settings were frozen (a fingerprint of the code, the star list and every threshold was written down before any result was read) and the search covered 5,064 star-sectors (every star in every sector TESS watched it) in about 30 minutes, with no errors. It found 604 real dips, of which 186 passed the automatic checks. The honest part: the same search on upside-down copies of the same curves, which cannot hold planets, found 174. So the real-curve count is hardly above the false-alarm count, and nothing in the totals says planets are in there. Looking at the 8 strongest isolated dips, the two strongest turned out to be the sloping edge of a long, deep eclipse of the star pair itself, 0.8 to 1 day from the catalogue eclipse. Our rule drops events within 0.35 days of an eclipse, and those eclipses are wider than that. One star showed 33 dips in a regular pattern repeating every 9.06 days in every sector, which looks like another eclipsing pair sharing the same pixels. The other dips were slow drifts that only one of the three data products showed. Not one is a candidate. The list of events stays on the PC and only totals are published.
  15. We fixed what the first search showed, and searched again. Two new flags, both set from physics and applied to the real and the upside-down curves alike. First: a dip is flagged if it touches an eclipse of the star pair, with the eclipse length worked out from the star's size and its orbit (the old rule used a fixed 0.35 days, too short for big stars). Second: a star-sector with three or more dips is flagged as a variable star or a second eclipsing pair, because a planet circling a pair that orbits in 5 days or more needs at least about 15 days per orbit, so at most two transits fit in a 27 day sector. The search itself was unchanged (the second run gave the identical 2,642 events), so only the flags moved. Three of the eight events we had looked at, including the two strongest, are now flagged as touching an eclipse; the other five still pass. The honest result: the real dips that pass fell from 186 to 64, but the upside-down control fell from 174 to 90, so real is still not above the control. One caution: I chose these rules after seeing the first results, so this version is now frozen and must not be tuned further on these stars. We also checked catalogues: 6 of our stars are TESS planet candidates or known planet hosts, 53 are in the TESS eclipsing binary catalogue, and a sixth known circumbinary host (Kepler-1660) is in our list that we have not used as a control. Literature points to one big missing check: a flat baseline test (a transit is a box, a ramp is not). Full notes are in research/stage3/learnings-2026-10-27.md.
  16. We added a flat-baseline test, and the picture got clearer. A planet crossing a star makes a box: the light just before and just after it sits at the normal level. A ramp or the edge of an eclipse does not, and a dip with no data on one side cannot be checked at all. So the search now flags any dip whose flux before or after is off by more than half its depth, or that lacks data on a side. We measured the cost first by injecting fake box dips into 160 random star-sectors: 97.7% of them were kept. The search itself again returned the identical 2,642 events; only flags changed. The results: the real dips that pass fell from 64 to 15 (186 in the first run), and the upside-down control fell from 90 to 38 (174 at first). Real is still below the control at every signal-to-noise bar from 7 to 12, so there is no sign of planets at this detection level. The surprise: more than half of everything the detector finds sits at the edge of a data segment (the start of an orbit or next to a gap), which is where the false alarms live. Of the 8 strongest events we had looked at, 6 are now flagged and 2 remain (a weak dip and a messy drift); neither is a candidate. The honest conclusion for now: the next gain is in how we handle noise (a correlated-noise correction to the signal-to-noise), not in more flags. The fix queue for the next version is in research/stage3/FIX-QUEUE.md.
  17. We labelled the leftovers and measured what the filters cost. None of the 15 real dips that pass all checks sits on a star that TESS already lists as a planet candidate or that is a known planet host, and none is on a star in the TESS eclipsing binary catalogue. So no catalogue explains them, which does not make them real. Stars with three or more dips in one sector have more uniform dip depths among the real curves (68%) than among the upside-down ones (42%), which probably means real eclipse-like structure, though we did not test that statistically. I also wrote a test for a regular period and then removed it: with thousands of trial periods, any three events fit some period by luck, so it could not tell structure from noise. To know what the filters cost real planets, we injected 1,548 fake dips (boxes and gently sloped ones, 4 to 14 hours long, strong ones) into 160 random star-sectors: 86% survive the eclipse and baseline flags. That is a ceiling, because the other flags and the second-product check remove more, and faint dips were not tested. A sixth known planet host in our list, Kepler-1660, produced no dip that passes the checks.
  18. A fourth version, and a correction to my own diagnosis. I had said our signal-to-noise was probably inflated by correlated noise. Reading the code showed that is wrong: the detector already divides each dip by the measured scatter of the same kind of dip across the whole light curve, which includes correlated noise. What remains is heavy tails (flares, ramps) and noise that changes along a sector. So I replaced that idea with three new flags, with the search itself again unchanged: a dip is flagged if the strongest upside-down dip in the same light curve is at least as strong (a fair local contest with no setting), if it falls within a day after data resumes (this costs 14% of the timeline), or if it touches an eclipse whose width we now take from the TESS eclipsing binary catalogue for 40 stars. Result: the real dips that pass are 12 and the upside-down ones 33, so still nothing above the control. A clue: the strongest dip in a light curve is more often an upside-down one (22% of real dips are beaten by one, against 13% the other way). That fits upward spikes such as flares being bigger than downward ones, which means the upside-down control probably overstates false alarms for dips. So "real is below the control" is expected from noise alone and proves nothing either way; the honest statement is only that no signal is visible. A scrambled control, which does not flip the sign, is the next test.
  19. We tested the noise itself, and wrote it all into the book. The question was whether upward spikes make the upside-down test too harsh. We counted raw dips with no rules at several strengths on 900 random star-months: the upside-down side had 1.25 times as many dips at a low bar and 2.3 times as many at our bar of 7. Planets would have pulled that ratio down, and it went up. So noise is lopsided, the control is harsh, and there is no sign of a planet at any strength. I also dropped the "scrambled control" idea after reading the source: it shuffles big blocks of time but keeps a single dip, so it cannot test a search for single dips. And I corrected one of my own notes: in the very first version the real side was slightly higher (186 against 174), which the later rules explained. The book has a new page, The first real search, with what we found, how the tool changed, our chances (roughly 1 in 10 that a findable planet is still hiding, my rough arithmetic) and what comes next. New sections in Chapters 7, 8, 9 and 10, two new lessons in Chapter 15, 13 glossary words, new check questions in Levels 3, 5 and 6 of the learning track, and 12 new rows in the claims register keep the learning track current.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (measure the claim): advice is a claim. Some claims have a number that can contradict them, such as a contrast ratio, a character count or a list of characters in a file. For those, checking with a tool beats reading, because a tool can say no. A contrast ratio compares the brightness of text and its background; 7 to 1 means the lighter is seven times brighter once a small allowance is added to both. Black on white is 21 to 1. A character map is the list of characters a font file can draw; if a character is missing, the device quietly borrows one from another font.

Idea (an honest label on every claim): the font report marked some facts as verified and some as estimates, and the estimates were true estimates. That is the standard we hold ourselves to: say which is which.

Idea (decide before you build): the learning-path review ended with three questions for you, not with code. Changing the order of a book changes how you learn, and that is your call.

Idea (make new code rebuild an old answer): before trusting new code, ask it to reproduce a result you already trust. Our Stage 3 preparation rebuilt the published Stage 2 numbers exactly (36 real events cut to 12, 7, 7, 4, 4, 4 and 1), and a re-run of the five known stars gave identical events. If either had differed, the new code would have been wrong, not the old result. This is called a regression test.

Idea (a flag is not a deletion): a rule such as "this event sits near a known eclipse" marks the event and moves it to a lower tier. It never throws the event away, because a real planet can cross at an awkward moment.

Idea (count the kind of mistake, not only the score): "93% right" hides that a missed planet, a false alarm and a mislabelled glitch cost the hunt different things. A miss loses a candidate, a false alarm wastes a check, and a glitch taken for a dip is the one that could fool us. Sort the misses by kind before judging anyone, a person or a program.

Idea (prove a test can say no): a test that has never failed has not shown it works. After the new layout test passed, we widened the reading column in a scratch copy and the test named every page it broke. Only then did we trust its pass.

Idea (let the interval choose the word): a rate is an estimate, and the 95% confidence interval is the span of true rates it fits. If the whole span is on the good side of a target, say so. If the span crosses the target, say that too. With 32 quiet curves even zero false alarms cannot show the true rate is under 10%, because the interval still reaches 10.7%. About 35 curves with none are needed. More curves, not a kinder sentence, are what move a result.

Idea (size a picture by its shape, not by the window): a plot's height is set by its aspect ratio, the height divided by the width. A share of the window makes the same plot tall on one screen and flat on another, so the dips change shape. Fix the ratio, then add a floor and a ceiling so it is never too small to read or too big to see whole.

Idea (reserve the space before you need it): if a button appears only after an answer, leave its slot empty from the start. Then the page does not jump under your finger when it arrives.

Idea (one fact, one place): a results page is clear when each number appears once, next to the line it is judged against. Repeating a fact in three lists does not make it safer, it only hides the one number you came for.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• List the missing characters of a font file (needs pip install fonttools brotli): python -c "from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont as T; cm=T('book/docs/assets/fonts/inter-latin-wght-normal.woff2').getBestCmap(); print([c for c in 'σμΔ≈≥' if ord(c) not in cm])"
  • Run node book/tools/test_eyes.mjs and read the new score-line check. Break the line You got ${right} of ${n} right. in book/docs/assets/eyes-core.js and see the test fail.
  • Open the two reviews in research/compass-reviews/: 2026-10-27-font-advice-report.md and 2026-10-27-learning-spine.md.
  • Open book/data/path.yml and read the track: list: it is the learning path. Move a chapter to another level there and python book/tools/test_shape.py refuses it until docs/learn/index.md agrees.
  • From the pipeline folder run ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe test_stage3_prep.py and read the line that says the Stage 2 numbers are identical. Change PH_D in stage3_core.py and watch that test fail.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found: the book's fonts have no Greek or math symbols (checked by reading the files). Two of the three font pairings in the report also lack Greek in the version Google serves. Four chapters sit outside every learning level.
  • Decided: on the test page you chose Atkinson Hyperlegible Next at the smallest size. It has no Greek letters in the version Google serves, so the redesign must add a small Greek and math set (σ, μ, Δ, ≈ and a few more) and test it.
  • Not found out: whether the fonts are why you dislike the look. It could also be the bright text on dark, the crowded layout on a PC, or both. The font test page is how we separate those.
  • Not tested: the font page has been checked for script errors but not yet looked at on your phone. The new score line is covered by tests on a local copy of the book, not on your device.
  • Found (hunt): the eclipse-phase rule never covers more than 28% of any star's timeline, because the shortest binary period is 5 days. Of the 136 stars with an unmeasured eclipse shape, 80 show a clear eclipse and 56 do not; those 56 would be searched last.
  • Not decided: the Stage 3 plan mentions a search for pairs of dips, but nothing for it is built. It needs your decision before the run.
  • Found (Eyes): in the first standard sitting your score went from 77% in the first two test rounds to 90% or more in every test round from the fourth on, and the last third of a round scores as well as the middle (83%) and above the first third (78%), so there is no sign of tiredness. Dips at strength 6.5 and above were found 84% to 98% of the time; below 6.5 only 47%, which is roughly under the search's own cut of 7, so that is the limit of the data and not a flaw in you.
  • Not tested (Eyes): every dip so far is a fake. The standard test and the hard test each still need a second day to count, and the real-candidate mode has had no rounds yet. Two rounds on a second device are too few to compare it with the first.
  • Not tested (F4): the new fonts, the PC chapter layout and the Eyes layout were measured by script and looked at in one window (the Eyes layout at five sizes), not yet on your iPhone or your own PC. A window between 1100 and 1120 pixels still gets the phone layout, a little later than the 1100 we drew.
  • The real search ran (item 14), once, with settings frozen first. Nothing in it is a planet candidate yet, and no event has been checked by a human.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. A font file lacks the character σ. What does your phone do when a page asks for it?

It quietly draws σ from another font on the phone. Nothing breaks, but the letter can look slightly different from the text around it.

2. Why was it better to calculate the contrast of the brass colour than to look at it?

A calculation gives a number that can contradict the claim (2.9 against a rule of 7). Looking only gives an impression, and our eyes forgive low contrast on a bright screen.

3. Why did we re-run the five known stars through the new code before searching the rest?

To prove the new code returns the same events as Stage 2. Then any difference in Stage 3 comes from the new rules, not from a slip in the code.

4. Why is a single score such as 93% not enough to judge how well someone spots dips?

Because the wrong answers differ in kind. Missing a faint dip, calling a quiet curve a dip and mistaking a jump for a dip each cost the hunt something different, so the misses must be sorted by kind first.

docs.title: 28 October 2026: check the rival before you copy it
docs.text:
Field note · day 10 · about 5 min

In plain words

You asked for an outside audit of one question: should we build a faster, learning-based search, or keep improving ours and test it against a professional tool? All three passes are done. Pass 1 studied a professional tool called mono-cbp, without running it. The most useful finding was small and countable: our 549 stars and their 512 stars overlap on only 30. Pass 2 studied VarWISE, a machine-learning catalogue, and found it is built for a very different job. Pass 3 weighed the options and recommends improving our own search, with mono-cbp as a small yardstick. Then you said go on v5, so we ran a better version of our own search and measured, for the first time, how faint a dip it can see. Then you said to go ahead with the yardstick test and to build the pair search, so we ran the professional tool on 30 shared stars and linked dips across sectors.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We read the paper and the code, not a summary of them. The team (Davies and others, 2026) searched 512 eclipsing binaries, 3,808 light curves in all, and found one weak candidate. I checked those numbers against the paper and against the table in their code repository, which holds exactly 591 starting stars before their last cuts.
  2. We checked the licence. The code is GPL-3.0. That is a "share alike" licence: you may use and change it, but a program that includes its code must be shared under the same terms. Our plan says MIT for our code, and no licence file exists yet, so nothing is locked in. The safe route is to run their tool on its own and never copy its code into ours (LIKELY, not legal advice).
  3. We counted the overlap with a script. Only 30 of our 549 stars are in their 591-star table VERIFIED. Our stars are fainter (middle brightness 12.45 against about 10.2 for theirs), and 70 of ours have binary periods under 7 days, which they left out. Of our six known circumbinary planet hosts, only Kepler-1647 is in both lists.
  4. We found that their paper and their code may differ. The paper describes an MCMC fit when it compares a transit with other shapes. The code appears to use a least-squares fit instead (LIKELY: I read the source through a summary, not line by line). If so, "benchmark against mono-cbp" means benchmarking the code, not reproducing the paper's exact numbers.
  5. We fixed one of our own sentences. The page The first real search said "we can search others they did not", which suggests most of the 4,584 are still open. Their 512 are the long-period, well-separated ones, so the rest are mostly close, overlapping or short-period systems. The line now says what is true and names the comparison as the next step.
  6. You set a working rule. Tiny changes such as a wording fix, a claim row or a field note are mine to make. Big things and decisions still come to you first.
  7. Pass 2: we read the VarWISE papers, and the two paper numbers in the audit prompt were swapped. arXiv 2409.15499 is VARnet, the detector (Paz 2024). arXiv 2605.19059 is VarWISE, the catalogue built with it (Paz and others 2026). VarWISE is not a planet search. It lists 1.9 million variable objects found in infrared data from a space telescope called NEOWISE, which watches each patch of sky for a few days about every six months. VARnet was trained on about a million fake light curves and checked on only 231 real objects, 48 of them eclipsing binaries. It is very fast, about 52 millionths of a second per source, because it was built for hundreds of millions of sources. Our whole 549-star search took about 40 minutes of machine time, so speed is not our problem.
  8. Pass 3: we compared three options and wrote the report. Option A is to improve our own search (test faint dips, search longer dips, mask eclipses before flattening). Option B is to run mono-cbp on a small shared set as a yardstick. Option C is to build a learning-based engine like VarWISE. The report recommends A first with B as a small side test, and C only if certain conditions are met later, such as tens of thousands of light curves or a few hundred human-labelled events to learn from. The full report, with the table, the benchmark plan and the cost of each step, is in research/audit-2026-10-28-report.md. Nothing in it is built yet, and the choice is yours.
  9. v5: we searched longer dips and measured how faint a dip we can see. The search now also tries a 20 hour box (the longest before was 15 hours). We first proved that the old settings still reproduce the Stage 2 numbers exactly, then froze the new settings and re-ran all 549 stars (5,082 star-months, no errors). First-tier events: 14 in the real curves against 35 in the upside-down copies (v4 was 12 against 33). The upside-down copy finds about 2.25 times more dips than the real one at our bar, so noise alone would give about 15.6 real events, and we got 14. There is still no sign of a planet. The new measurement: we hid fake dips of graded depth in 240 random star-months. An 8 hour dip is found 61% of the time when its depth is 10 times the scatter of 8 hour averages, 22% at 8 times and 2% at 6 times, and the checks then remove about a fifth of the ones found. So a faint planet could be hiding: below about 8 times that scatter the search is nearly blind.

  10. We corrected our own number. I had called 82.7 to 86.4% the completeness of the search. That was only the share of found dips that pass the checks. Only 72% of the deep fakes were found at all, so the whole chain keeps about 62%. We also measured, on made-up data, that the 2 day smoothing window cuts a 20 hour dip to 57% of its depth (a 15 hour one to 68%). A longer window for long dips is queued as v6. We did not build the per-star false-alarm level: both controls we have fail for single dips, so it would have had no honest null.

  11. We ran the rival tool, on its own, on the same stars. You said go ahead, so mono-cbp now lives in its own folder outside our project, with its own Python environment, so its licence never touches our code. It took three tries to install, because it needs older versions of two maths libraries. Then we fed it our local copies of the 224 star-sectors of the 30 stars both searches share, and also the same files turned upside down. It finished in about 7.5 minutes each time on one core. It found 437 events on the real curves and 209 on the upside-down ones. Ours, on the same stars, found 41 and 46. Only 3 of our 41 events were also found by it, and none of its 144 stronger events were found by us. Those strong events are deep (about 1%) and short (about 4.5 hours), and half sit on three stars, which looks like leftover eclipses of the binaries, not planets. We did not look at any single event. The honest reading: the two tools count different things, so a bigger number is not a better tool.

  12. A known planet is a better judge than a count. Instead of arguing over counts, we gave both tools the same question: do you find the published transits of TOI-1338 b? Our normal input (a cleaned version of the flux called PDCSAP) found 4 of the 8 transits that have data. The same files read as plain SAP flux found 7 of 8 VERIFIED. Either one alone finds all 8, because they fail in different sectors. mono-cbp found 7 of 8, but its own vetting step called 6 of them a sinusoid, not a transit, with the default settings VERIFIED. That led to a wider check on the 224 star-sectors: the noise is about equal on average, but SAP is clearly quieter than PDCSAP in about a quarter of the sectors, and clearly noisier in about one in eight VERIFIED. This is the most useful thing the yardstick gave us. You said go, so item 14 below is what we built; it also shows that the quarter does not carry over to the whole campaign.

  13. Pair search, and a print I changed. You said build it, so a first version now links dips of one star that sit in different sectors and have similar depth and length, and runs the same rule on the upside-down copies. Result on the frozen run: none of the 14 clean real dips pair up (the upside-down copy has 2 such pairs, noise alone would give 0.3). My first print looked very different: 10 real pairs against 2. I then changed two things, and I am saying so here. It used every product's version of a dip, but the report judges a dip by its best product; and it counted pairs, but several similar dips on one star make many pairs that are not independent. Both fixes lowered the real count. I saw the higher number first, and that is recorded. The pair search can only get interesting with weaker dips, which needs a new frozen search.

  14. You said go on item 15, so the search now reads both versions of the light. The new version (v6) is the old v5 search, copied unchanged, plus a second pass over the SAP flux of the best SPOC or TESS-SPOC file in 1,420 star-sectors. A dip that both versions find keeps its old record, and a dip only SAP finds is added. We first proved that the old settings still reproduce Stage 2 exactly (74 and 298 events), that the new rules fail when broken on purpose (7 of 7), and that the new reader finds TOI-1338 b as before (4 of 8, 7 of 8, 8 of 8 together). Does it help? A little, for faint dips. We put the same fake dip into both versions of 240 random star-sectors. An 8 hour dip at 7 times the noise was found 10% of the time with PDCSAP, 11% with SAP and 16% with either VERIFIED. The gain sits where SAP is the quieter version, and that was only about 3% of these star-sectors, not the quarter we saw on the 30 stars in item 12. The list got longer, not better. Tier 1 went from 14 real and 35 upside-down to 33 real and 36 upside-down: the SAP half added 19 real and 1 upside-down VERIFIED. That looks like a signal, and we do not trust it. In SAP the raw counts of real and upside-down dips are equal at strength 7 and upside-down is the larger side at strength 10, so there is no raw excess; four of our checks remove a larger share of the upside-down events than of the real ones (the repeater check removes 55% of the upside-down and 25% of the real), while the two eclipse checks hit more real events LIKELY. Sixteen of the 19 sit in four late sectors and 12 share a moment with other stars, which looks like the camera, not a planet (LIKELY; nobody looked at any event). The pair search on the union again finds nothing. We did not tune v6 to make this go away; a fairer version of the cross-star check and a fair control for SAP are queued as v7.

  15. You said do the fair check first, so the control is now fair where it can be, and the SAP list shrank. We built v7, which has two parts and no new search. First, a fairer burst check. The old check asked: do upside-down events on other stars happen at this moment? That is a fair question for an upside-down event and an odd one for a real dip, so it removed more of the control than of the data. The new check asks every event, real or upside-down, the same question of the same pool: do three or more other stars on the same camera have an event of either kind within 0.1 days? In the SAP half it now hits real and upside-down dips in almost equal shares (78% and 75%), where the old check hit 52% and 66% VERIFIED. Second, a physical test. A dip that only the SAP flux finds must also show, at strength 3 or more, in the PDCSAP flux of the same file. A planet should, because it is the same pixels with the camera drift taken out. A camera glitch that PDC corrected should not. Fake dips pass this test 87% of the time (193 of 222) VERIFIED. The result. Tier 1 went from 33 real and 36 upside-down (v6) to 21 and 32. The SAP half went from 19 real and 1 upside-down to 7 and 0 VERIFIED. Is that evidence? No. The control is still not fair for the SAP half. After the camera check and the eclipse checks, 67 real and 41 upside-down dips are left. The repeater and flat-baseline checks then leave 14 and 2, and one more leaves 14 and 0, so the control has nothing left to compare with. Also, the PDCSAP flux shows 19% of the real SAP-only dips and 23% of their upside-down mirror images, so real dips are not confirmed more often than mirrors LIKELY. That test is a filter, not a proof: about 1 dip in 5 made of pure noise passes it by chance. Half of the 14 clean dips (7) pass it, which is more than the one in five overall, but mirror images with only one flag pass it almost as often (9 of 19), so cleaner stretches simply agree more. One mistake of ours, fixed. A line of the v6 report judged all 33 real events against a ratio that was measured only on PDCSAP flux, and it said the chance of this from noise was 0.00. It now covers the PDCSAP half only: 14 real events against 15.6 expected, chance 0.69 VERIFIED. I did not catch it when I wrote v6. While building the new test I also found that the "PDCSAP" curve we search quietly fills gaps from the plain flux, so the new test reads PDCSAP without that fill. Nobody has looked at any event.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (compare on the same stars): two searches can only be compared where they looked at the same stars with the same kind of data. Before planning a benchmark, count the stars both sides share. Ours shares 30.

Idea (an open licence is a rule about code, not about ideas): a licence such as GPL-3.0 controls copying and sharing the code. Running a program on your data, and reading the method in its paper to write your own version, are different acts from pasting its code into yours. When a licence matters, say which of these you are doing.

Idea (a paper and its code can disagree): a paper tells you what the authors say they did, the code tells you what runs. When a result is going to be a benchmark, read the code too.

Idea (recovery is two numbers): how often a fake dip is found, times how often a found dip survives the checks. Quote both. A single "completeness" figure hid that only 72% were found at all.

Idea (a smoothing window is a trade): flattening a light curve removes slow drifts, but it also eats part of any dip that is long compared with the window. A wider window keeps more of the dip and more of the drift. The right width depends on the dip.

Idea (fast for whose problem?): a tool's speed matters only against the size of your own job. VARnet's speed answers a sky-wide job of hundreds of millions of sources. Ours is 549 stars, so a faster engine would save minutes, while a better test of what we miss could change what we find.

Idea (a benchmark needs an answer key): a test of a planet finder needs planets whose answer is known. Only six of ours are known, and one of those is shared with them, so a fair test will need extra known cases and injected fake planets.

Idea (a known answer beats an agreement count): two tools that count different things will disagree, and a disagreement does not say who is right. A published planet with known transit times is a fixed answer both can be graded on.

Idea (two inputs can fail on different days): the cleaned flux and the plain flux of the same star each lost some transits the other kept. Using both and keeping the union is cheap insurance, as long as you record which one saw what.

Idea (say which number you saw first): if you change a method after seeing a result, write down the first result and why you changed it. A change that lowers a surprising number is fine only if the reasons were true before you looked.

Idea (a fair control treats a thing and its mirror the same): a control only tells you something if every check is applied to it exactly as it is applied to the data. If one check looks at the mirror images of other stars only, it will treat a real dip and its mirror differently, and the difference looks like a discovery. Give the real event and its mirror the same question and the same pool, and the difference goes away. What stays is the part of the noise that is truly lopsided, and no check can fix that: it needs a different kind of control, or a test that does not need a control, such as asking whether a second version of the same light also shows the dip.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Count our stars and their brightness: from the project folder run .venv\Scripts\python.exe -c "import pandas as pd; g=pd.read_csv('targets/g1_targets.csv',comment='#').drop_duplicates('tic'); print(len(g), round(g.tmag.median(),2), (g.p_bin_d<7).sum())". It prints 549, 12.45 and 70.
  • Read the licence yourself: open the mono-cbp repository and its LICENSE file, then the GNU GPL questions page.
  • Read the paper, section by section: the sample cuts, then the vetting steps.
  • Rerun our pair search on the frozen events: from the project folder run cd pipeline, then ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe pair_search.py. It prints counts only.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (VERIFIED): the paper's sample numbers match the paper and the table in the code. The licence is GPL-3.0. The overlap is 30 stars, and Kepler-1647 is the one shared known host.
  • Found (LIKELY): the code and the paper differ on how the shapes are compared; the licence advice above.
  • Found (UNCERTAIN): in the paper's numbers, real light curves gave about 2.3 times as many raw events as upside-down ones, while ours gave fewer real than upside-down. That is my own arithmetic and I do not know the reason yet. Running both on the 30 shared stars would test it.
  • Found (VERIFIED, from the papers): VarWISE uses infrared NEOWISE data with epochs about six months apart, has no planet class (its two eclipsing classes are Algol-type and W UMa-type), and reports no completeness. Its authors say so: completeness is not quantified. Sampled objects labelled eclipsing-detached were 100% eclipsing (262 checked by eye). VARnet reports no false-alarm rate, only precision and recall on 231 curated objects. No code release was found for either.
  • Found (LIKELY): a learning-based search for our job would need many labelled planets to learn from. We have six known hosts, and the professional team tested 14. So it would have to train on fake planets only, as VARnet did, and check on a handful of real ones.
  • Found (v5, VERIFIED by our own runs): the old settings still reproduce Stage 2 exactly; the 20 hour box finds 20 hour dips the old grid could not; the real count stays below the control at every strength bar; the faint-dip table above (research/stage3/faint_recovery_v5.txt).
  • Found (LIKELY): planets close to our detection bar are far more likely to be missed than the earlier "1 in 10 still hiding" suggested, because that figure used the keep rate of strong dips.
  • Not tested (v5): faint-dip recovery with every check included (second product, bursts), the same table converted to planet size for a typical star, and a longer smoothing window for long dips. Nobody has looked at any of the 14 first-tier events.
  • Not tested: we did not install or run mono-cbp, and nobody has compared its results with ours. The last 59,000 characters of the VarWISE paper were not read. The decision between improving ours, benchmarking theirs, or building a learning-based search is recommended in pass 3 but not made: it is yours.
  • Found (VERIFIED, our own runs, item 11): mono-cbp 0.1.9 installs and runs on 224 star-sectors in about 7.5 minutes per pass; on the 30 shared stars it finds 437 events on the real curves and 209 on the upside-down ones, against our 41 and 46. Update to the UNCERTAIN note above: mono-cbp's real-to-upside-down ratio on these stars is 2.1, close to the paper's 2.3, while ours is 0.9. Its extra real events are deep and short, and I think leftover eclipses (LIKELY, NOT TESTED).
  • Found (VERIFIED, item 12): on TOI-1338 b, our PDCSAP input finds 4 of 8 testable transits, SAP finds 7 of 8, and together 8 of 8. mono-cbp detects 7 of 8 but its default vetting labels 6 of them as sinusoids. SAP is more than 20% quieter than PDCSAP in 23% of the 224 star-sectors (LIKELY for the wider sample: 30 stars only; cause unknown).
  • Found (VERIFIED, item 13): the pair search finds no pair among the 14 clean real dips. No excess over noise in the wider class either (5 real stars with a pair against 11 expected).
  • Not tested (items 11 to 13): the same injected dips in both tools (the fair recovery comparison); mono-cbp with the paper's own data product and settings; a repeat run to prove it reproduces; the pair search with weaker dips and with the check that shorter periods fall in data gaps. The SAP change to our search is not built.
  • Found (VERIFIED, our own runs, item 14): v6 leaves every v5 event unchanged and adds 550 real and 488 upside-down SAP-only dips. The same fake dip is found about 1.3 to 2 times as often by either version as by PDCSAP alone at 6 to 8 times the noise, and almost never added at 10 times. The numbers are in research/stage3/sap_recovery_v6.txt and aggregate_v6.txt.
  • Found (LIKELY, item 14): the 19 extra tier-1 dips are mostly camera effects, not planets, and the upside-down copy is not a fair control for SAP (four of the checks remove a larger share of it, and SAP noise is lopsided the other way). NOT TESTED: the fair cross-star check, a fair control for SAP, and any look at an event.

  • Not tested (item 14): SAP in the 1,599 files that sit in sectors where QLP is the best product; the recovery table with every check included; the second-product rule for SAP against other files. The v5 numbers (14 real against 35 upside-down) stay the reference.

  • Found (VERIFIED, our own runs, item 15): the common-moment check treats real and upside-down dips alike in the SAP half (78% against 75%, p = 0.27). With it and the PDCSAP test, tier 1 is 21 real against 32 upside-down, and the SAP half adds 7 real and 0 upside-down. The PDCSAP half stays at 14 real against 32 upside-down (v6: 35). Numbers in research/stage3/sap_fairness_fd788be04650.txt and aggregate_v7.txt.

  • Found (LIKELY, item 15): the 7 SAP-only first-tier dips are SAP camera effects, not planets. The upside-down copy runs out after the repeater and flat-baseline checks, so it cannot serve as a null for the SAP half, and the PDCSAP flux does not confirm real dips more often than mirrors (19% against 23%). Three of the 7 sit in sectors 76 and 80 (16 of the earlier 19 sat in sectors 75, 76, 80 and 82). Pair search on the new list: nothing.
  • Not tested (item 15): how many true dips survive the whole chain in SAP (the recovery table with every check), SAP in the 1,599 files that sit in sectors where QLP is the best product, a control that keeps SAP's lopsided noise, and any look at an event. The v5 numbers (14 real against 35 upside-down) stay the reference; v7 gives 14 against 32 for the same half.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we count shared stars before planning a benchmark?

A comparison is only fair where both searches looked at the same stars with the same data. With 30 shared stars, the test is small, and that shapes what we can conclude.

2. Running a GPL program on your data is not the same as copying its code into yours. Why does that matter for our licence plan?

The share-alike rule bites when code is combined into another program. Running their tool separately and citing it keeps our own code free to be MIT. This is likely but not legal advice.

3. A tool takes about 50 millionths of a second per star. Why does that not make it the better choice for 549 stars?

Speed matters against the size of the job. Ours already finishes in about 40 minutes, so the limit on what we find is how well we test and vet events, not how fast we compute.

4. A fake dip is found 61% of the time, and 80% of the ones found pass the checks. What share does the search keep?

About 49% (0.61 times 0.80). Quote both numbers, because a figure that only counts the dips that were found hides how many were never found.

5. A paper says one method, the code uses another. What do you do before building a benchmark?

Read the code too, then decide whether you are testing the paper's method or the repository's. The two can give different numbers.

6. mono-cbp found 437 events and we found 41 on the same stars. Why is that not a result about which tool is better?

The tools count different things: their strength scale is different, they search to much weaker dips, and their strongest events look like leftover eclipses. Only 3 events overlapped. A fixed answer, like a known planet, is a fairer judge than a count.

7. Our PDCSAP input found 4 of 8 TOI-1338 b transits and SAP found 7 of 8. What do you do with that?

Do not swap one for the other: either alone finds all 8 only when combined, because they fail in different sectors. Queue a change to search both and keep the union, record which product saw each event, and re-prove that the old numbers are unchanged before freezing it.

8. A first print showed 10 real pairs against 2, then a fixed version showed 0 against 2. What should you write down?

Both numbers, and why the method changed: the first print used the wrong unit (every product, and pairs instead of stars). Say that you saw the higher number first, so a reader can judge whether the change was fair.

docs.title: 29 October 2026: how small a planet could we have found?
docs.text:
Field note · day 11 · about 6 min

Correction, 10 Nov 2026

An audit found that our fake-planet tests added the fake dips after the step that hides eclipses, or used a mask built from clean light. A real planet's dip is already in the light when that step runs, and the step can delete it. With the fakes put in first, the old search lost 4 to 6 of every 10 strong dips, and the loss grows as the binary gets slower (most lost dips are in 5 to 14 day binaries, because most of our data are there). So every "found X percent", "smallest planet" and "floor" number on this page is an upper limit. "No excess of real dips over noise" is not changed. The full story.

In plain words

We have searched 549 stars with Vesper and found nothing above noise. Today we asked the question that gives that result its meaning: if a planet had been there, how big would it have to be for us to catch it? We pasted thousands of fake dips into our own data and ran the whole frozen search on them. The answer is humbling. Only the biggest planets would have been caught, so "we found nothing" is a weak statement. It is still an honest one, and now it has numbers.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We checked the fill. Our "cleaned light" input fills some missing readings from the raw light. We counted: 0.67% of readings are filled, and a filled reading sits inside 8.5% of real dips and 7.8% of upside-down dips, so it affects both sides alike VERIFIED. No error was swallowed in secret. The run logs hold zero errors; the only silent skips are 21 QLP files with no safe time windows.
  2. We found a wrong name. Of the 14 first-tier dips we called "cleaned light", 10 sit on QLP's raw flux, because QLP has no cleaned column before sector 56 VERIFIED. The comparison with the upside-down copy still holds, since both sides use the same flux, but the word "cleaned" was wrong. The briefing now says so, and the code gets the new name at the next freeze.
  3. We built a test that sends fake dips through the whole chain. It pastes the same fake dip, at the same time and depth, into every file of a star-sector. Then the unchanged frozen code runs: search, checks, second look, raw-light twin, union and tiers. With nothing pasted in, it reproduces the real events in all 299 star-sectors tried, so it is the same machine.
  4. We ran 14,352 fake dips in 299 random star-sectors, 4 lengths, 6 depths, each as a dip and as a mirror bump. Even a very deep dip (18 times the noise) is seen almost every time, but only 44% to 64% end in the first tier. Half are recovered at about 11 times the 8 hour noise, which is about 8,000 parts per million for the middle star LIKELY.
  5. We compared that with the known planets. We asked the NASA Exoplanet Archive for the sizes of known circumbinary planets and worked out the deepest dip each could make. Against 8,000 ppm only Kepler-16 b clears the bar for a middle star. Against the quietest bright stars (about 3,100 ppm) roughly half of the transiting ones do.
  6. We tested the mirror. A fake dip and its mirror bump pass through the chain almost equally well: 32% against 34% LIKELY. That supports using the upside-down copy as a control, within about two points.
  7. We counted the next star list (G2). The catalogue we already had gives 895 new stars under the same rule as G1. I first guessed 1 to 4 GB of downloads. The query said about 28 GB, because every star has many sectors. I wrote my wrong guess down next to the right number.
  8. One slip of mine: I pointed the browser at a PDF link and it offered to save the file on your PC. You cancelled it and nothing was saved. The new rule: I ask before touching any file link.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (injection and recovery): to learn what a search could find, paste fake signals of known size into real data and count how many come out. The fraction is the completeness. It must be measured through the whole chain, because a dip that is found can still be thrown out by a check.

Idea (a ceiling is information): at 18 times the noise a dip is seen 99% of the time but kept only about 55% of the time. The missing 45% is the price of the checks. A check that protects against false alarms also loses real dips, and both sides of that trade should be measured.

Idea (depth first, radius second): a planet's dip depth is its radius over the crossed star's radius, squared, times the share of light that star gives. We know neither number for a binary, and the catalogue radius describes the blend. So we report depth and length first, and planet size only as a labelled range.

Idea (a name can mislead): "cleaned light" turned out to be mostly raw QLP flux. When a label hides what is inside, count the contents.

Idea (a guess is not a measurement): my 1 to 4 GB guess was wrong by a factor of seven. A cheap query replaced it. Check before you plan around a number.

Idea (test the control, not only the data): the upside-down copy is only a fair control if every check treats it like the data. The mirror test checks that for planet-like signals.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Print the whole recovery table from the saved rows: from the project folder run cd pipeline, then ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe chain_recovery.py summary v7.
  • Re-run the faithfulness test: ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe chain_recovery_test.py (a few minutes). It prints PASS lines.
  • Look up a known planet's size yourself on the NASA Exoplanet Archive and compute (planet radius over star radius) squared.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (VERIFIED, our own runs): the fill is 0.67% and acts on both sides alike; the whole chain recovers at most 44% to 64% of very deep dips; half are recovered at about 11 times the 8 hour noise; a dip and its mirror bump are recovered about equally (32% against 34%).
  • Found (VERIFIED by counting): 10 of the 14 "cleaned-light" first-tier dips are on QLP raw flux.
  • Found (LIKELY): a null on our 549 stars excludes giant planets and quiet bright stars, not typical circumbinary planets. The depths of the known ones are upper bounds, because their star's companion adds light.
  • Found (LIKELY): the flat-baseline check costs long dips most (10% of short dips, 37% of 20 hour dips), probably because the 2 day smoothing window absorbs part of a long dip. NOT TESTED.
  • Not tested: planet size from the real crossed-star radius and light share (not in our table); the 90% level (our depth grid stopped at 18 times the noise); false alarms per check set against dips lost per check; any real event. Nobody has looked at any event.
  • Uncertain: whether the saved TESS binary catalogue's periods were redone with the later sectors; how much of the 28 GB is 20 second files.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. A fake dip is seen at SNR 7 in 99% of runs but ends in the first tier 55% of the time. Where did the other 44% go?

Into the checks. Flags for data gaps, ramps, a non-flat baseline, eclipses, shared moments and repeats move a found dip to tier 2. Quote both numbers: found, and kept.

2. Why do we report dip depth before planet radius?

Depth is what we measure. Radius needs the crossed star's radius and its share of the light, and for a binary the catalogue gives neither. The radius is a range with assumptions, not a measurement.

3. Kepler-16 b makes a dip of about 14,000 ppm and Kepler-38 b about 500 ppm. Which could our search catch at 50%?

Only the first, and only around a middle star (50% needs about 8,000 ppm). The second is far below even the best case of about 3,100 ppm.

4. What does the mirror-bump test check?

Whether the checks treat a dip in the real path and a bump in the upside-down path alike. If they do, the upside-down copy is a fair control for planet-like signals. Here they differ by about two points, which is small.

5. We guessed 1 to 4 GB and the query said 28 GB. What was the mistake?

I used the sector count in the table, but the archive holds every sector TESS has released since. When a number drives a plan, measure it with the cheapest check first.

6. Why was 'cleaned light' a misleading name?

10 of the 14 dips it covers sit on QLP's raw flux column, since QLP has no cleaned column before sector 56. The label hid what was inside. Count the contents before trusting the name.

docs.title: 30 October 2026: we tried to make the filter better and learned why it will not be free
docs.text:
Field note · day 12 · about 6 min

In plain words

Since 29 October we have been asking one question: how can our filter find smaller circumbinary planets? Today we finished a long round of tests. Every idea we tried either found more fake dips as fast as it found more real ones, or found nothing new. That is a result, not a failure of effort. It tells us the filter is close to a balance: more planets caught costs more false alarms, about one for one. The choice of how many false alarms to accept is yours, not a thing to tune quietly.

docs.title: What we did, and why
docs.text:
1. We asked whether the next big step (stacking) was worth it. Stacking means adding up several transits of the same planet to see a smaller one. Before doing any work we wrote a rule down: skip it if the known planets are mostly slow and stacking reaches few of our stars. We read the NASA Exoplanet Archive: 14 transiting circumbinary planets are known, 11 of them have periods over 100 days, and the middle one is about 194 days. At that period stacking reaches only about 10% (first star list) to 19% (second list) of our stars, even in the best case. The rule said skip, so we skipped.
  2. We looked at the false alarms that get through. They are not white noise. Our nine checks stop about 98% of upside-down events, at every brightness; the 2% that get through look like short glitches. On both star lists the 3 hour box held most of them: 14 of 32 and 16 of 25.
  3. We read how a published search handles the same problem (the mono-cbp paper, Davies and others, 2026). It reaches the same conclusion: most things that pass are leftover systematics. Its extra check, that a dip must survive many smoothing settings, costs up to two thirds of the shallow long dips, the same trade we had already measured.
  4. We tested a box floor. The idea: drop the 3 hour box, the false alarms go, we gain room to loosen another check. We wrote the rule and the hope before running anything. Results on both lists: with the box gone, the false alarms did not go. They moved to the 4 hour box. The count of short-box survivors stayed at 17 on the first list and went from 20 to 16 on the second. The floor cost 7 to 8 points of recovery for 4 hour dips and bought nothing significant. Combined with the looser step check, false alarms stayed at 10 to 12 per 1,000 star-sectors against our limit of 8.
  5. We filed every result, including the failures, in the plan, the version table and a shopping list for the next version. Nothing was tuned on the results, and nobody opened a real event.

docs.title: The idea behind it
docs.text:
Idea (write the rule before the result): the stacking gate and the box-floor test were written down first, so the answer could not bend to what we wished. The gate said skip, and we skipped; the test said no gain, and we recorded no gain.

Idea (an exchange rate): for every idea that did work, the gain in real dips was about equal to the gain in false alarms. When a filter sits at a balance like that, the right question is not "which trick?" but "how many false alarms are we willing to pay for how many planets?"

Idea (where something is found is not what causes it): the false alarms were most common in the 3 hour box, so I blamed the box. But when we removed it, the same glitches were found by the next box. A count by box shows where a thing is caught first. To find the cause you must ask: if I remove this, where does it go?

Idea (check a borrowed rule's conditions): I used a published "smoothing window is three times the transit" rule in a case where its conditions did not hold (our smoothing does not mask the dip). It cost a quarter of an 8 hour dip. Read when a rule applies, not just what it says.

docs.title: How you could do it yourself
docs.text:
• Look up the periods yourself on the NASA Exoplanet Archive (filter for circumbinary, transiting) and take the median.
  • Re-run the box-floor test: from the project folder run cd pipeline, then ..\.venv\Scripts\python.exe test_vopts.py (a minute; it prints PASS lines). The full runs take hours at low priority.
  • Read the three tables in research\stage3\VESPER-VERSIONS.md and look at the last column: it is the reason each idea was not accepted.

docs.title: What we found, and what we did not
docs.text:
• Found (CONFIRMED, our own runs and the archive): stacking reaches few stars at the periods most known planets have; the false alarms that get through are short glitches; dropping the 3 hour box moves them to the 4 hour box; every option tried trades about one real gain for one false alarm.
  • Found (LIKELY): the filter is near a balance, so only new information (a physical duration limit per star, or repeat transits for the short-period planets) can improve it without a cost.
  • Not tested: a physical duration limit per star (needs star radii, a download that needs your yes); a higher bar only for the shortest boxes; the repeated-transit check for the short-period end; any real event.
  • Uncertain: how many of our binaries can show a 3 hour transit at all.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
1. Why did we write the stacking rule before reading the archive?

So the answer could not be shaped by what we hoped for. A rule written first is a test; a rule written after the result is a story.

2. The 3 hour box held most false alarms. Why did removing it not help?

The false alarms are short glitches, and the 4 hour box catches the same glitches. The box showed where they were found, not what made them.

3. What does 'one for one' mean here, and why does it matter?

For each extra real dip we recover we also let through about one extra false alarm. So there is no free improvement left in tuning; the number of false alarms we accept has to be decided on purpose.

4. Why is it good news that the idea failed?

We know why, we filed it so nobody repeats it, and the next step is clear. A clean, measured null is the win condition of this project.

docs.title: Later the same day: the v8 design
docs.text:
With the testing round finished, we wrote the next version. Three choices were open (how many false alarms to accept, whether to keep the shortest box, how to weigh the dip lengths). For each one I kept the rule we had written before the tests, because changing a rule after seeing which options fall just short of it is a quiet way of tuning on results. You can still change any of them before the freeze.

So v8 is the old filter plus one new check: the orbit-locked flag. A dip that repeats in another sector at exactly a whole number of the binary's own orbits, with the same length and depth, is most likely a leftover eclipse, not a planet, because a planet keeps its own clock. On the development stars it removes 49 events on 7 stars, the real-minus-control excess drops from +65 to +20, and it costs about 0.8% of planted fake planets. On the first star list it changes nothing. The check is built, tested and gives exactly the numbers we measured offline. It is not frozen yet: the freeze and the sealed stars wait for your go.

5. Why is a dip that repeats at a whole number of binary orbits suspicious?
