docs.title: 2.1 Orbits and periods
docs.text: Unit 2 · What makes a dip · Lesson 2.1 · 15 min

docs.title: Orbits and periods
docs.text:
Same two stars, now watched for four TESS sectors in a row: about 106 days.

Count the deep drops. Some reach about minus 43%, some only about minus 35%. Do the two kinds take turns?

docs.title: A clock in the sky
docs.text:
The drops come back again and again, and they come in two kinds. The deeper ones (about 45% at their 2-minute bottom) happen when one star passes in front of the other; the shallower ones (about 36%) when it is the other way round. Astronomers call the deeper kind the primary eclipse and the shallower kind the secondary eclipse.

Primary and secondary eclipse. The deeper and the shallower of the two eclipses that a pair of stars makes in each orbit.

The time from one primary eclipse to the next is the time the stars take to go once round each other: the period, written \(P\). Every orbit, the same lineup repeats (almost exactly: over years this oval orbit slowly turns, which the discovery paper measured), so a period is a very exact clock.

Period (\(P\)). The time for one full orbit. Here, the time from one primary eclipse to the next.

Look closely and you will notice that not every orbit shows both eclipses. Our script finds the middles of five primary eclipses, at days 2507.395, 2527.053, 2546.710, 2586.028 and 2605.685 on the TESS clock. The one that should come between 2546.710 and 2586.028, near day 2566.4, fell in a gap in the data (a gap of about 2.8 days, most likely while TESS sent its data home). One secondary eclipse is lost the same way. Gaps like these are why a single planet crossing can be missed even when the telescope is looking at the right star.

Worked example: measuring the period

Step 1. Take the first and the last primary eclipse. Days 2507.395 and 2605.685.

Step 2. Subtract. \(2605.685 - 2507.395 = 98.290\) days.

Step 3. Count the orbits in between. The gaps between neighbours are about 19.7, 19.7, 39.3 and 19.7 days. The 39.3 is two orbits (the missing eclipse), so the total is \(1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5\) orbits.

Step 4. Divide. \(P = 98.290 / 5 = 19.658\) days.

Why not just subtract two neighbours? Each eclipse time has a small error. Spreading that error over five orbits makes the period's error five times smaller. The discovery paper gives 19.7 days, the same value rounded.

docs.title: How far apart are the stars? Kepler's third law
docs.text:
About 400 years ago Johannes Kepler found a rule linking how long an orbit takes to how big it is. In the form astronomers use for stars:

\[ P^2 = \frac{a^3}{M} \]

Kepler's third law. In these units: period in years, size in astronomical units, mass in Suns. It works for planets around the Sun, for two stars, and for a planet around two stars.

Here \(P\) is the period in years, \(M\) is the total mass of everything inside the orbit in Suns, and \(a\) is the size of the orbit in astronomical units (AU): 1 AU is the distance from the Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km. For an oval orbit, \(a\) is half of its long axis, the average of the closest and the farthest distance.

Astronomical unit (AU). The Earth's average distance from the Sun, about 150 million km. A ruler for orbits.

Check it on the Earth: \(P = 1\) year and \(M = 1\) Sun, so \(a^3 = 1\) and \(a = 1\) AU. Right.

We want \(a\), so we turn the law around: multiply both sides by \(M\) and take the cube root, the number that multiplied by itself three times gives what is under the root (the cube root of 8 is 2, because \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\)):

\[ a = \sqrt[3]{M P^2} \]

Worked example: the two stars of TIC 172900988

The discovery paper gives the stars' masses: 1.238 and 1.202 Suns, so \(M = 2.440\).

Step 1. Period in years. \(19.658 / 365.25 = 0.05382\) years.

Step 2. Square it. \(0.05382^2 = 0.002897\).

Step 3. Times the mass. \(2.440 \times 0.002897 = 0.007069\).

Step 4. Cube root. \(\sqrt[3]{0.007069} = 0.192\) AU.

The two stars sit about 0.19 AU apart: half of Mercury's distance from the Sun. That is about 41 Sun radii, while each star's radius is only about 1.4 Sun radii. Close, but far from touching. (0.19 AU is the orbit's average size: on this stretched oval the distance swings between about 0.11 and 0.28 AU.)

Your turn, half done: the planet's orbit

The planet goes round both stars once in about 200 days (the paper allows six values between 189 and 204). It feels the pull of both stars together, so \(M = 2.440\) again. Step 1: \(200 / 365.25 = 0.5476\) years. Step 2: \(0.5476^2 = 0.2998\). Finish steps 3 and 4.

Your turn. The size of the planet's orbit, in AU:

Worked solution

Step 3: \(2.440 \times 0.2998 = 0.7316\). Step 4: \(\sqrt[3]{0.7316} = 0.90\) AU.

The rule: \(a = \sqrt[3]{M P^2}\), with \(P\) in years and \(M\) the total mass inside the orbit. The planet circles both stars at about 0.9 AU, almost five times farther out than the stars are from each other. That is no accident: Unit 4 shows why a planet cannot orbit two suns too closely.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: A pair of stars makes two eclipses each orbit, a deeper primary and a shallower secondary; the time between two primaries is the period. Measure it across many orbits to make it exact; gaps in the data can hide whole eclipses. Kepler's third law, \(P^2 = a^3 / M\), turns a period and a mass into the size of an orbit.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. A star pair's first primary eclipse is at day 100.0 and its fourth at day 160.0, with none missing between. What is the period?

Worked solution

From the first to the fourth eclipse there are 3 orbits (1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4). \(160.0 - 100.0 = 60.0\) days, and \(60.0 / 3 = 20.0\) days.

2. The last primary eclipse in the plot is at day 2605.685 and the period is 19.658 days. When is the next primary eclipse, on the TESS clock?

Worked solution

\(2605.685 + 19.658 = 2625.343\). Predicting eclipses like this is how astronomers plan observations, and how our search masks eclipses out of the light before looking for planets.

3. A planet orbits a star of 1 Sun mass at 4 AU. How long is its year?

Worked solution

\(P^2 = a^3 / M = 4^3 / 1 = 64\), so \(P = \sqrt{64} = 8\) years. (Jupiter, at 5.2 AU, takes about 12 years.)

4. Kepler-16 b, the first planet found crossing two suns, orbits stars of 0.69 and 0.20 Sun masses every 229 days. How big is its orbit, in AU?

Worked solution

\(M = 0.69 + 0.20 = 0.89\). \(P = 229 / 365.25 = 0.627\) years, \(P^2 = 0.393\). \(M P^2 = 0.89 \times 0.393 = 0.350\). Cube root: \(a = 0.70\) AU, about the distance of Venus from the Sun.

5. Two orbits have the same size \(a\), but one goes round 8 times more mass. How many times shorter is its period?

Worked solution

With \(a\) fixed, \(P^2\) is proportional to \(1 / M\). Eight times the mass makes \(P^2\) eight times smaller, so \(P\) is \(\sqrt{8} = 2.83\) times smaller. More mass pulls harder, so the same orbit is travelled faster.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Eclipse times and the period: TESS sectors 44 to 47, 2-minute light curves of TIC 172900988 (MAST); middles of the eclipses (halfway through the time below 90% of normal) and the fitted period 19.658 days measured by our scripts on 15 Nov 2026 (book/tools/lesson_plots.py and a check script). Both missing eclipses (days 2566.4 and 2538.9) fall in mid-sector data gaps.
  • Masses, period and planet periods: Kostov et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.08614): "P = 19.7 days", M1 = 1.2384 and M2 = 1.2019 solar masses, planet period "188.8, 190.4, 194.0, 199.0, 200.4, or 204.1 days".
  • Kepler-16: Doyle et al. 2011 (arXiv 1109.3432): stars "20% and 69% as massive as the sun", planet on "a nearly circular 229-day orbit".

docs.title: 2.2 How long a dip lasts
docs.text: Unit 2 · What makes a dip · Lesson 2.2 · 14 min

docs.title: How long a dip lasts
docs.text:
The planet's second crossing from lesson 1.4 again. This time, ignore the depth and look only at the time.

Touch where the light starts to fall and where it is back. How many hours apart are they? (Read the days, then multiply by 24.)

docs.title: Width of the star, speed of the planet
docs.text:
A planet's dip lasts as long as the planet takes to cross the face of its star. That is a simple travel-time problem, the same as a car crossing a bridge: time = distance / speed.

The distance is about the width of the star, \(2 R_\star\) (a little more, because the planet's own disc must get fully on and off; we will ignore that small extra). The speed comes from the orbit. In one period \(P\) the planet travels once round a circle of radius \(a\), a distance of \(2 \pi a\), so its speed is \(2 \pi a / P\). Divide:

\[ T = \frac{2 R_\star}{2 \pi a / P} = \frac{P}{\pi} \cdot \frac{R_\star}{a} \]

Transit duration (\(T\)). How long a dip lasts. This simple form assumes a circular orbit, a crossing straight through the middle of the star, and a star that stands still.

The formula says three things. A longer year (bigger \(P\)) means a longer dip. A bigger star (bigger \(R_\star\)) means a longer dip. A wider orbit (bigger \(a\)) means a shorter one, because the star looks smaller from far away... except that \(P\) also grows with \(a\) (lesson 2.1), and that wins: far-out planets make long dips.

Same units. \(R_\star\) and \(a\) must be in the same unit before you divide. 1 AU is 215 Sun radii.

Worked example: the Earth crossing the Sun

Seen from far away, how long would the Earth's dip across the Sun last?

Step 1. The ratio \(R_\star / a\). The Sun's radius is 1, and 1 AU is 215.0 Sun radii, so \(R_\star / a = 1 / 215.0 = 0.004651\).

Step 2. \(P / \pi\). \(365.25 / 3.1416 = 116.26\) days.

Step 3. Multiply. \(116.26 \times 0.004651 = 0.5407\) days.

Step 4. Into hours. \(0.5407 \times 24 = 13.0\) hours.

An alien astronomer watching the Sun would see the Earth's 84 ppm dip last about 13 hours, once a year.

Your turn, half done: a hot Jupiter

A giant planet orbits a Sun-like star every 3 days, at \(a = 0.0407\) AU (from Kepler's law). Step 1: \(a\) in Sun radii is \(0.0407 \times 215.0 = 8.75\), so \(R_\star / a = 1 / 8.75 = 0.1143\). Finish: work out \(P / \pi\), multiply, and give the duration in hours.

Your turn. Duration of the hot Jupiter's dip, in hours:

Worked solution

\(P / \pi = 3 / 3.1416 = 0.955\) days. Times \(0.1143\): \(0.109\) days. Times 24: 2.62 hours.

The rule: \(T = (P / \pi)(R_\star / a)\). Close-in planets make short dips: a few hours, against 13 for the Earth and about 30 for Jupiter (33 if Jupiter's own size is counted).

docs.title: Around two suns, the clock runs differently
docs.text:
Now try the formula on our planet. From lessons 1.2 and 2.1: \(P \approx 200\) days, \(a \approx 0.90\) AU \(= 193.5\) Sun radii, and the star it crosses in this plot is the smaller one, 1.31 Sun radii. So \(R_\star / a = 1.31 / 193.5 = 0.00677\), \(P / \pi = 63.7\) days, and \(T = 63.7 \times 0.00677 = 0.431\) days, about 10 hours.

But the plot at the top shows a dip lasting only about 6 hours (our rough reading: the light stays more than 1,200 ppm low for about 6 hours). Why so short?

Two of the formula's assumptions can fail here. First, the planet may not cross through the middle of the star: an off-centre path is a shorter chord, and a crossing about 0.8 star radii off-centre would alone turn 10 hours into 6. Second, the star does not stand still. Each star swings round the pair's centre every 19.7 days, at a speed our numbers put near 50 km/s, about as fast as the planet itself travels (also near 50 km/s). If the star happens to move towards the planet as it crosses, their speeds add up and the crossing is quick. If the star moves the same way as the planet, it is almost a race, and the crossing can last much longer. From one dip we cannot tell which effect matters more; the discovery paper fits both with a full model of the three bodies. What is certain is that around two suns every dip has its own length, and its spacing and depth change too. Unit 4 takes this apart, because it is the very thing our search has to cope with.

The speeds. Star: about half of the 0.19 AU separation, once round in 19.7 days. Planet: 0.9 AU, once round in about 200 days. Both come to about 50 km/s.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: A dip lasts as long as the planet takes to cross its star: \(T = (P / \pi)(R_\star / a)\) for a circular orbit straight through the middle of a still star. The Earth would make a 13-hour dip, a hot Jupiter a 2 to 3-hour one. Around two suns the star moves too, so each crossing has its own length.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. A planet orbits a star of one Sun radius every 10 days, at \(a = 0.09\) AU. How long is its dip, in hours?

Worked solution

\(a = 0.09 \times 215.0 = 19.35\) Sun radii, so \(R_\star / a = 1 / 19.35 = 0.0517\). \(P / \pi = 10 / 3.1416 = 3.183\) days. \(T = 3.183 \times 0.0517 = 0.165\) days \(= 3.95\) hours.

2. Same planet, same orbit, but the star is twice as wide. How many times longer is the dip?

Worked solution

\(T\) is proportional to \(R_\star\): twice the star, twice the crossing time. (The depth, though, falls to a quarter, because depth goes with \(1 / R_\star^2\).)

3. Our planet's dip lasts about 6 hours, and the light curve has one point every 30 minutes. How many points does the dip hold? (Why this matters: it is how many points the dip's average uses, the N of lesson 1.4.)

Worked solution

\(6 \times 60 / 30 = 12\) points. With 2-minute data it would be 180 points, but each would collect 15 times less light and so be noisier by \(\sqrt{15}\); for pure photon noise the two effects cancel and the dip is no clearer. What faster points do give is the dip's shape: ingress and egress become visible instead of blurred.

4. Around two suns, the star happens to move in the same direction as the planet during a crossing. Is the dip longer or shorter than the still-star formula says? (One word.)

Worked solution

Longer. The planet has to catch up with a star that is running away from it, so their relative speed is small and the crossing takes more time.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The duration formula and its assumptions (circular orbit, central crossing; the full form also has the planet's own size and the crossing's offset from the centre): Winn 2010, "Transits and Occultations" (arXiv 1001.2010).
  • 1 AU = 215.03 Sun radii (IAU nominal solar radius 695,700 km; 1 AU = 149,597,871 km).
  • Our planet's numbers: Kostov et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.08614) for the masses and periods; the orbit size from Kepler's law (lesson 2.1); the 6-hour reading and the speeds of about 50 km/s are our own rough calculations from those numbers (15 Nov 2026), not values from the paper.

docs.title: 2.3 Why stars differ
docs.text: Unit 2 · What makes a dip · Lesson 2.3 · 15 min

docs.title: Why stars differ
docs.text:
The four sectors from lesson 2.1 again. Look only at the bottoms of the drops.

The two kinds of eclipse do not reach the same depth. Before reading on, guess why: is one star bigger, hotter, or something else?

docs.title: Two numbers make a star's light
docs.text:
Our two stars are nearly twins, but not quite. The discovery paper measured them:

  • Star 1: radius 1.3827 Suns, surface at 6,050 K.
  • Star 2: radius 1.3124 Suns, surface at 5,983 K.
  • The Sun, for comparison: radius 1, surface at 5,772 K.

Kelvin (K). Temperature counted from absolute zero. Add 273 to degrees Celsius; at these heats the difference hardly matters.

How much light a star sends out in total is called its luminosity. It depends on just two things: how much glowing surface the star has, and how hot that surface is.

Luminosity (\(L\)). The total light a star sends out every second, in all directions. Here in Suns: \(L = 1\) is the Sun.

The surface is easy: a sphere's area grows with its radius squared, \(R^2\). A star twice as wide has four times the glowing skin.

The heat is the surprise. Every square metre of a hot surface glows, and the glow grows with the temperature to the fourth power, \(T^4\). Make a surface twice as hot and each square metre shines \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 16\) times brighter. This is the Stefan-Boltzmann law, and it is why a small change in temperature matters far more than a small change in size.

Stefan-Boltzmann law. Light from each square metre of a hot surface grows as \(T^4\). Put together with the area: \(L = R^2 \, T^4\), with \(R\) and \(T\) both measured against the Sun.

Put the two together, measuring both against the Sun:

\[ L = R^2 \times T^4 \]

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
Answer each before moving on. They build the idea one step at a time.

a. A star has twice the Sun's radius and the Sun's temperature. How many times more light does it give?

b. Now a star the Sun's size but twice as hot. How many times more light?

c. Two stars of the same size. You cover the same patch of each. Covering which one hides more light: the hotter or the cooler? (One word.)

Worked example: how bright is star 1?

Step 1. Radius squared. \(1.3827^2 = 1.912\).

Step 2. Temperature against the Sun. \(6050 / 5772 = 1.0482\).

Step 3. To the fourth power. \(1.0482^4 = 1.207\). (Square it, then square again: \(1.0482^2 = 1.0987\), \(1.0987^2 = 1.207\).)

Step 4. Multiply. \(L = 1.912 \times 1.207 = 2.31\) Suns.

Notice what happened: the star is only 5% hotter than the Sun, yet that alone gives 21% more light per square metre. Its larger size gives the rest.

Your turn, half done: star 2

Step 1: \(1.3124^2 = 1.7224\). Step 2: \(5983 / 5772 = 1.0366\). Finish: raise 1.0366 to the fourth power, then multiply.

Your turn. Star 2's luminosity, in Suns:

Worked solution

\(1.0366^2 = 1.0745\), \(1.0745^2 = 1.1545\). Then \(1.7224 \times 1.1545 = 1.99\) Suns.

The rule: \(L = R^2 \, T^4\), both measured against the Sun. Together the pair gives \(2.31 + 1.99 = 4.30\) Suns of light, which is what TESS sees as one point of light.

docs.title: Back to the two eclipses
docs.text:
So why are the drops different? Your answer to c says part of it: when the hotter star is hidden, more light goes. But here the two stars are so close in temperature that each square metre of star 1 is only about 5% brighter than star 2's (\((6050 / 5983)^4 = 1.046\)). That cannot by itself turn one eclipse into 45% and the other into 36%.

The rest comes from the orbit. Lesson 2.1 showed it is a stretched oval: the stars are closer together at one eclipse than at the other. Seen from Earth, the front star then passes across the back star along a different line each time, a little more centrally at one eclipse than at the other, so the two discs overlap by different amounts. Star sizes, temperatures and orbit shape all leave their mark in the depths, which is how the discovery paper could measure every one of them from the light curve and the stars' speeds together.

Colour. Hotter stars also look bluer and cooler ones redder. Unit 3 shows why, from how hot things glow.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: A star's total light is \(L = R^2 \, T^4\) in Sun units: the area of its glowing skin times the fourth power of its temperature. Temperature wins: 5% hotter gives 21% more light from each square metre. Our two stars give 2.31 and 1.99 Suns. Their eclipses differ in depth partly because one is a little hotter, but mostly because the stretched orbit makes them overlap by different amounts.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. A red dwarf has 0.2 of the Sun's radius and a surface at 3,000 K. Its luminosity, in Suns?

Worked solution

\(3000 / 5772 = 0.520\); \(0.520^4 = 0.0730\). \(0.2^2 = 0.04\). \(L = 0.04 \times 0.0730 = 0.0029\) Suns: about 340 of them to match one Sun. Red dwarfs are the commonest stars near the Sun, yet even the nearest star of all, Proxima Centauri, a red dwarf, is far too faint to see without a telescope.

2. A star the Sun's size gives 16 times the Sun's light. How many times hotter than the Sun is its surface?

Worked solution

Same radius, so \(T^4 = 16\), and \(T = 2\): twice as hot, about 11,500 K. A blue-white star.

3. Two stars of the same size: one at the Sun's 5,772 K, the other at 6,050 K. How many times more light does the hotter one give?

Worked solution

\((6050 / 5772)^4 = 1.0482^4 = 1.21\). Less than 5% hotter, 21% more light.

4. In our pair, what makes most of the difference between the two eclipse depths: the temperatures or the orbit? (One word.)

Worked solution

The orbit. The temperatures differ by only about 1%, giving about 5% in brightness per square metre. The stretched orbit makes the stars overlap by different amounts at the two eclipses, and that makes most of the difference.

docs.text:
• Star radii and temperatures: Kostov et al. 2021, the discovery paper (arXiv 2105.08614); radii from its abstract, temperatures \(6050 \pm 100\) K and \(5983 \pm 100\) K from its stellar properties table (read 15 Nov 2026).
  • The Sun's surface temperature, 5,772 K: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 (nominal solar effective temperature).
  • Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf at visual magnitude about 11, far below the naked-eye limit of about 6 (to be confirmed by the fact-check).
  • \(L \propto R^2 T^4\) (the Stefan-Boltzmann law): any introductory text, for example OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 5 "Radiation and Spectra" (the book, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
  • Different overlap at the two eclipses of an oval orbit: Winn 2010, "Transits and Occultations" (arXiv 1001.2010), where the crossing offsets of the two eclipses differ by the orbit's shape. That this, and not temperature, explains most of the depth difference here is our own reasoning from the paper's numbers (15 Nov 2026).

docs.title: 2.4 Light from two stars at once
docs.text: Unit 2 · What makes a dip · Lesson 2.4 · 15 min

docs.title: Light from two stars at once
docs.text:
The planet's second crossing, the one from lessons 1.4 and 2.2. This time, think about the depth.

Lesson 1.4 measured this dip at about 2,655 ppm. The planet is as wide as Jupiter, and Jupiter across the Sun makes about 10,600 ppm. Why is this dip so much shallower?

docs.title: One point of light, two stars inside it
docs.text:
TESS cannot see our two stars apart. They are only about 0.19 AU from each other, which from Earth spans less than a thousandth of an arcsecond, while one TESS pixel is 21 arcseconds wide. (Only the sharpest instruments on Earth, which combine several telescopes, reach that fine; TESS is nowhere near.) So every point on our light curve is the light of both stars added together.

When the planet crosses star 2, it blocks part of star 2's light only. Star 1 keeps shining as if nothing happened. The dip is real, but it is measured against the light of both stars, so it looks shallower. Astronomers call this dilution: the dip is watered down by light that the planet never touched.

Dilution. Extra light from another star (a partner, or an unrelated star in the same pixels) that makes a dip look shallower than it really is.

Arcsecond. A tiny angle: 1/3,600 of a degree. The full Moon is about 1,800 arcseconds across.

The rule is one multiplication. If the crossed star gives a fraction \(s\) of all the light we receive:

\[ \text{seen depth} = s \times (\text{fraction of the crossed star's light blocked}) \]

When the planet is fully in front of the star, and we treat the star's disc as evenly bright, that blocked fraction is the area ratio from lesson 1.2, so

\[ \text{seen depth} \approx \left( \frac{R_p}{R_\star} \right)^2 \times s \]

(While the planet is still sliding on or off the edge it blocks less, and a real star's disc is a little darker at its edge than at its centre, so this is roughly the depth at the dip's middle.)

The share \(s\). The crossed star's light divided by the total: 1 if it shines alone, \(\tfrac12\) for two identical twins.

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
a. Two identical twin stars. What share \(s\) of the light does one of them give? (A number.)

b. A planet would block 10,000 ppm of one twin's light. How deep is the dip we see, in ppm?

c. If we forget the twin and read the shallow dip as if the star shone alone, will we think the planet is bigger or smaller than it really is? (One word.)

Worked example: what should the dip be?

The paper gives the planet 11.25 Earth radii and star 2 1.3124 Sun radii (one Sun radius is 109.08 Earth radii).

Step 1. Radius ratio. \(11.25 / (1.3124 \times 109.08) = 11.25 / 143.16 = 0.07859\).

Step 2. Depth if star 2 shone alone. \(0.07859^2 = 0.006176\), that is 6,176 ppm.

Step 3. Star 2's share of the light. From lesson 2.3: star 2 gives 1.99 Suns, the pair 4.30. So \(s = 1.99 / 4.30 = 0.463\).

Step 4. Seen depth. \(6{,}176 \times 0.463 = 2{,}860\) ppm.

Lesson 1.4 measured 2,655 ppm. The simple rule gets within about 8%, and that is about as close as it can be: the planet's size is known to within about 4%, which alone moves the predicted depth by about 8%. We have not measured what makes up the rest. Possible contributors: the star's disc is darker at its edge than at its centre (which can push the depth either way, depending on where the planet crosses), our 12-point average includes some points near the dip's edges, and TESS sees red light, where the two stars' shares differ slightly from their shares of all light (lesson 2.3 counted all colours).

Your turn, half done: forgetting the partner

Suppose nobody knew star 1 was there. We see 2,655 ppm and think star 2 shines alone. Step 1: \(\sqrt{0.002655} = 0.05153\), so the planet looks 0.05153 times as wide as star 2. Finish: star 2 is 143.16 Earth radii wide; how many Earth radii would we give the planet?

Your turn. The planet's size if we forget dilution, in Earth radii:

Worked solution

\(0.05153 \times 143.16 = 7.38\) Earth radii: a planet between Neptune (3.9) and Saturn (9.4) in size. Correct for dilution first (divide the depth by 0.463: 5,734 ppm, ratio 0.0757) and it becomes 10.8 Earth radii, close to the paper's 11.25.

The rule: divide the seen depth by the share before you work out the planet's size. Forget dilution and every planet looks too small.

docs.title: The same trick can fool us
docs.text:
Dilution also works the other way, and it is one of the most common ways a search gets fooled. TESS pixels are large: each one is about 21 arcseconds across, so light from faint stars nearby often lands in the same pixels as our target. Now imagine one of those faint stars is itself an eclipsing binary, with eclipses 50% deep. If that star gives only 1% of the light in our pixels, its eclipse shows up in our light curve as \(50\% \times 0.01 = 0.5\%\): 5,000 ppm, exactly the depth a giant planet would make.

Blend. A dip that comes from another star mixed into the same pixels, not from the target. The checks in Unit 7 exist to catch blends.

That is why every candidate dip gets the pixel and neighbour checks in Unit 7: is the dip centred on our star, or on a neighbour? For our pair, the TESS Input Catalog estimates that other stars add only about 0.05% to the light in the pixels, so blends are not a worry here. The partner star is.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: When two stars share one point of light, a planet crossing one of them makes a dip diluted by the other's light: seen depth = \(s\) times the fraction of the crossed star's light that is blocked, roughly \((R_p/R_\star)^2 \times s\), with \(s\) the crossed star's share. Star 2 gives 46% of our pair's light, which turns a 6,176 ppm dip into about 2,860. Forget dilution and planets look too small; an unseen faint eclipsing binary in the same pixels can, diluted, look just like a planet.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. A planet would block 10,000 ppm of its star's light, but that star gives only 20% of the light we receive. How deep is the dip we see, in ppm?

Worked solution

\(10{,}000 \times 0.2 = 2{,}000\) ppm.

2. A faint background star gives 1% of the light in our pixels and has eclipses 50% deep. How deep do they look in our light curve, in ppm?

Worked solution

\(50\% = 500{,}000\) ppm. Times \(0.01\): 5,000 ppm. A giant planet's depth, made by a star that is not our target at all.

3. Around two identical twin stars we see a 2,000 ppm dip. How deep would it be if the crossed star shone alone, in ppm?

Worked solution

Each twin gives \(s = 0.5\). Undiluted depth \(= 2{,}000 / 0.5 = 4{,}000\) ppm.

4. In a pair, the planet crosses the fainter star. Compared with crossing an equal-sized but brighter partner, is the dip deeper or shallower? (One word.)

Worked solution

Shallower. The fainter star's share \(s\) is smaller, so more of the light we see comes from the partner the planet does not touch.

docs.text:
• Planet and star radii: Kostov et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.08614), abstract; the planet first crossed the primary star, then 5 days later the secondary (the crossing in this lesson's plot). Contamination 0.000453 from the paper's table, quoting the TESS Input Catalog (read 15 Nov 2026).
  • 1 Sun radius = 109.08 Earth radii (IAU nominal values).
  • TESS pixels are about 21 arcseconds across: Ricker et al. 2015, the TESS mission paper (arXiv 1406.0151), table 1: one pixel is 0.35 by 0.35 arcminutes (checked by Codex 022).
  • Dilution and blends as false positives: any vetting guide; for the TESS case see the TESS mission paper above. Neptune 3.9 and Saturn 9.4 Earth radii: NASA planetary fact sheets (equatorial radii, rounded).
  • The 2,860 ppm prediction, its 8% gap and the 7.38 and 10.8 Earth-radii figures are our own arithmetic from the paper's numbers (15 Nov 2026).

docs.title: 2.5 Gravity from scratch
docs.text: Unit 2 · What makes a dip · Lesson 2.5 · 18 min

docs.title: Gravity from scratch
docs.text:
The two stars' clock from lesson 2.1: the deeper eclipse comes back every 19.7 days, again and again.

Nothing pushes these stars along, yet they keep going round. What keeps them moving, and what sets the 19.7 days?

docs.title: Falling, and missing
docs.text:
In lesson 2.1 we used Kepler's law, \(P^2 = a^3 / M\), as a rule handed down. Kepler found it in 1619 by staring at tables of planet positions, and he never knew why it worked. Isaac Newton found the why about 70 years later, and you can follow his argument with nothing more than the maths you already have.

Start with a thought experiment Newton drew himself. Stand on a very tall mountain and throw a stone sideways. It curves down and lands. Throw it faster and it lands farther away. Now throw it so fast that, as it falls, the round Earth curves away beneath it just as fast as it drops. It keeps falling and never lands. That is an orbit: falling all the time, and always missing. The astronauts on the space station are not floating because gravity is gone up there (it is about 90% as strong as on the ground); they float because they and their station are falling together.

Orbit. A path where an object falls towards another forever but moves sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

docs.title: The pull: Newton's law of gravity
docs.text:
Newton's second idea: every mass pulls every other mass, and the pull weakens with distance in a very particular way. Twice as far, a quarter of the pull. Three times as far, a ninth. This is the inverse-square law, and it is the same square as in lesson 2.3, for the same reason: whatever spreads out from a point is shared over a sphere whose area grows as the distance squared.

Inverse-square law. A pull (or a light) that falls as \(1/r^2\): double the distance, a quarter of the strength.

The pull on each kilogram of a planet, at distance \(r\) from a star of mass \(M\), is

\[ g = \frac{G M}{r^2} \]

where \(G\) is Newton's gravitational constant, the same everywhere in the universe. For the Sun, the product \(GM\) is measured very precisely: \(1.3271 \times 10^{20}\) in metres cubed per second squared.

\(G\). Newton's constant, \(6.674 \times 10^{-11}\) in SI units (the standard system of metres, kilograms and seconds; here m³ per kg per s²). Tiny: gravity is by far the weakest force, and only matters because stars and planets are so massive.

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
a. A planet moves to three times its old distance from its star. How many times weaker is the star's pull on it?

b. Look at \(g = GM/r^2\). Does the planet's own mass appear in it? (Yes or no.)

That answer b is Galileo's dropped balls all over again: a heavy and a light ball fall together, and a pebble and a giant planet at the same distance from a star follow the same orbit (as long as they are tiny next to the star).

docs.title: The speed an orbit needs
docs.text:
For a circle of radius \(r\), moving at speed \(v\), the pull needed to keep bending the path into the circle is \(v^2 / r\) per kilogram. In an orbit, gravity supplies exactly that pull:

\[ \frac{v^2}{r} = \frac{G M}{r^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v = \sqrt{\frac{G M}{r}} \]

Why \(v^2/r\). Faster means more bending each second, and a tighter circle means sharper bending. Both together give \(v^2/r\), a result Christiaan Huygens and Newton worked out in the 1600s.

Worked example: how fast is the Earth moving?

Step 1. The numbers. \(GM_\odot = 1.3271 \times 10^{20}\); \(r = 1\) AU \(= 1.4960 \times 10^{11}\) m.

Step 2. Divide. \(1.3271 \times 10^{20} / 1.4960 \times 10^{11} = 8.871 \times 10^{8}\).

Step 3. Square root. \(\sqrt{8.871 \times 10^{8}} = 29{,}780\) m/s.

Step 4. Into km/s. About 29.8 km/s: the Earth carries you round the Sun at 30 km every second, about 100,000 km every hour.

Your turn, half done: the planet around our two stars

It feels the pull of both stars, \(M = 2.440\) Suns, at \(r = 0.90\) AU (lesson 2.1). Since \(v = \sqrt{GM/r}\), compared with the Earth the speed changes by \(\sqrt{2.440 / 0.90}\). Step 1: \(2.440 / 0.90 = 2.711\). Finish: take the square root and multiply by 29.78 km/s.

Your turn. The planet's speed, in km/s:

Worked solution

\(\sqrt{2.711} = 1.647\), and \(1.647 \times 29.78 = 49.0\) km/s. This is the "about 50 km/s" lesson 2.2 used.

The rule: \(v = \sqrt{GM/r}\). More mass, faster orbit; farther out, slower.

docs.title: Kepler's law falls out
docs.text:
Now the period. One trip round the circle is a distance \(2\pi r\), done at speed \(v\), so \(P = 2\pi r / v\). Put in the speed and square both sides:

\[ P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2 r^2}{v^2} = \frac{4\pi^2 r^2}{G M / r} = \frac{4\pi^2}{G}\,\frac{r^3}{M} \]

That is Kepler's third law: \(P^2\) grows with \(r^3\) and shrinks with \(M\). The only extra piece is the constant \(4\pi^2 / G\). Measure \(P\) in years, \(r\) in AU and \(M\) in Suns, and that constant comes out as 1.00004: one, to better than a hundredth of a percent. That is no coincidence: the year and the AU are the Earth's own period and orbit size, and the Earth's mass is tiny next to the Sun's, so Kepler's law in these units must give about 1 for the Earth. That is why lesson 2.1 could write simply \(P^2 = a^3/M\).

The same law, read backwards, is how astronomers weigh things. Measure an orbit's size and period, and the mass inside it follows. The discovery paper weighed our two stars to better than 0.1% this way, from their eclipses and their measured speeds.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: An orbit is falling while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing. Gravity pulls each kilogram with \(GM/r^2\), weaker as the square of the distance, the same for a pebble and a planet. Making that pull bend the path into a circle gives the orbit speed \(v = \sqrt{GM/r}\): 29.8 km/s for the Earth, 49 km/s for the planet around our pair. Working out the period from that speed gives Kepler's third law, and turns every orbit into a scale for weighing stars.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. How fast would a planet orbit the Sun at 4 AU, in km/s?

Worked solution

\(v \propto 1/\sqrt{r}\). \(\sqrt{4} = 2\), so \(29.78 / 2 = 14.9\) km/s. (Jupiter, at 5.2 AU, moves at about 13 km/s.)

2. The space station flies about 400 km up, so \(r = 6{,}771\) km from the Earth's centre. For the Earth, \(GM = 3.986 \times 10^{14}\). First its speed, then its time for one orbit, in minutes.

Worked solution

\(r = 6.771 \times 10^6\) m. \(v = \sqrt{3.986 \times 10^{14} / 6.771 \times 10^{6}} = \sqrt{5.887 \times 10^{7}} = 7{,}673\) m/s. One orbit: \(2\pi r = 4.254 \times 10^{7}\) m, so \(P = 4.254 \times 10^{7} / 7{,}673 = 5{,}545\) s \(= 92.4\) minutes. The crew sees about 16 sunrises a day.

3. A planet orbits at the same distance as the Earth, but around a star four times the Sun's mass. How many times the Earth's year is its year?

Worked solution

\(P^2 = r^3/M = 1/4\), so \(P = 1/2\): half a year. A heavier star pulls harder, so the planet has to move faster to keep missing it, and goes round sooner.

4. Astronauts on the space station float. Is gravity missing up there, or are they doing something? Say in one word what they are doing.

Worked solution

Falling. Gravity there is about 90% of its pull on the ground. The crew and the station fall around the Earth together, so the floor never pushes back on their feet.

docs.text:

  • Kepler's third law, 1619 (Harmonices Mundi); Newton's cannon and law of gravitation, Principia (1687). Any history of astronomy, for example OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 3 "Orbits and Gravity" (the book, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0).
  • The stars' masses (to better than 0.1%): Kostov et al. 2021 (arXiv 2105.08614).
  • Space station altitude about 400 km, gravity there about 90% of the surface value (\((6371/6771)^2 = 0.885\)): our arithmetic; the station's real height varies, roughly 400 to 420 km.

docs.title: 3.1 What light is
docs.text: Unit 3 · Light itself · Lesson 3.1 · 15 min

docs.title: What light is
docs.text:
Every number in this book so far came from one thing: light from a star, counted by a camera. This plot shows what that camera can count.

The bottom axis is not time this time. It is colour, written as a number. Before reading on, guess: where is TESS blind, and where does it see best?

docs.title: Light is a wave
docs.text:
Light is a ripple of electric and magnetic fields travelling through space. Like a ripple on water, it has crests, and the distance from one crest to the next is its wavelength.

Wavelength (\(\lambda\), "lambda"). The distance from one crest of a wave to the next. For light it is tiny, so we measure it in nanometres (nm): one billionth of a metre.

Your eye reads wavelength as colour. Light of about 700 nm looks red, about 550 nm green, about 450 nm blue, and about 400 nm violet. That band, roughly 400 to 700 nm, is all your eye can see.

The rainbow does not stop where your eye does. Past red come longer waves, infrared, then microwaves and radio. Past violet come shorter ones, ultraviolet, then X-rays and gamma rays. All of these are the same thing, light, with different wavelengths. Lined up by wavelength they make the spectrum.

docs.title: Speed, wavelength and frequency
docs.text:
All light in empty space travels at the same speed, \(c = 299{,}792{,}458\) metres per second. As a wave passes you, crests arrive one after another. How many arrive each second is the frequency.

Frequency (\(f\)). How many crests pass a point each second. Unit: the hertz (Hz), one per second.

If each crest is \(\lambda\) apart and the wave moves \(c\) metres each second, then \(c / \lambda\) crests pass every second:

\[ c = \lambda \times f \]

Long waves, low frequency. Short waves, high frequency. The two always multiply to the same speed.

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
a. A micrometre is a millionth of a metre. How many nanometres fit in one micrometre?

b. Red light (700 nm) or violet light (400 nm): which has the higher frequency? (One word.)

c. How many times higher is violet's frequency than red's?

Worked example: the frequency of 1,000 nm light

Step 1. Metres. \(1{,}000 \text{ nm} = 1{,}000 \times 10^{-9} = 10^{-6}\) m.

Step 2. Divide the speed by the wavelength. \(f = c / \lambda = 3.00 \times 10^{8} / 10^{-6} = 3.00 \times 10^{14}\) Hz.

Three hundred million million crests every second. That is the reddest light TESS records well.

Your turn, half done: 600 nm

Step 1: \(600 \text{ nm} = 6.00 \times 10^{-7}\) m. Finish: divide \(3.00 \times 10^{8}\) by it.

Your turn. The frequency of 600 nm light, in Hz (you can type 5e14):

Worked solution

\(f = 3.00 \times 10^{8} / 6.00 \times 10^{-7} = 0.5 \times 10^{15} = 5.00 \times 10^{14}\) Hz.

The rule: \(c = \lambda f\), with the wavelength in metres.

docs.title: Back to the plot
docs.text:
Touch the curve. Below about 580 nm the share is zero: TESS is blind to green, blue and violet. It records best from about 600 to 950 nm, red light and the near infrared just past it, peaking near 720 nm where it keeps about 0.79 of the light that arrives. By about 1,050 nm it fades out again. Most of what TESS sees, your eye could never see at all.

Why build a camera like that? Small planets are easier to spot around small stars, because they hide a bigger share of the star. Small stars are cool, and cool stars shine mostly in red and infrared light. So TESS's builders made it see red. The smallest common ones, red dwarfs, make up about three quarters of the stars near the Sun. Lesson 3.2 shows why cooler means redder.

Response curve. For each wavelength, the share of arriving light an instrument records. It sets which colours a "brightness" number really counts.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: Light is a wave; its wavelength is its colour, and the eye sees only about 400 to 700 nm of a spectrum that runs from radio to gamma rays. All light moves at \(c\), so \(c = \lambda f\): shorter waves have higher frequencies. TESS counts light from about 600 to 1,000 nm, red and near infrared, best near 720 nm, because small planets are easiest to find around small stars, and small stars are cool and red.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. Read the plot: about what share of the light arriving at 1,000 nm does TESS record?

Worked solution

About 0.30. Touch the curve at 1,000 nm. The camera's sensitivity falls away fast past about 950 nm.

2. A star sends out a strong burst of green light at 530 nm. Would TESS's brightness numbers show it? (Yes or no.)

Worked solution

No. The response is zero below about 570 nm. TESS's light curves count only red and near-infrared light.

3. An FM radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz (\(10^{8}\) Hz). What is its wavelength, in metres? Radio is light too.

Worked solution

\(\lambda = c / f = 3.00 \times 10^{8} / 10^{8} = 3\) m. The same kind of wave as starlight, a few million times longer.

4. Small planets are easier to find around which kind of star, the reason TESS was made to see red? (Two words.)

Worked solution

Small stars. A small planet hides a bigger share of a small star, so its dip is deeper. Small stars are cool and shine mostly in red and infrared light, where TESS looks. The smallest common ones are the red dwarfs.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The TESS response curve: TESS instrument response function, version 2.0, R. Vanderspek, TESS Payload Operations Center, MIT, 2020, from the NASA TESS Science Support Center (downloaded 15 Nov 2026). Peak 0.785 at 722 nm, half of peak from 580 to 982 nm: our own reading of the file.
  • TESS's 600 to 1,000 nm band and why: Ricker et al. 2015, "The Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite", JATIS 1, 014003 (arXiv 1406.0151), section 3.4: "Enhanced sensitivity to red wavelengths is desired because small planets are more easily detected around small stars, which are cool and red." Red dwarfs (M0 to M5) as about three quarters of nearby stars: the same paper, section 3.3 (read 15 Nov 2026).
  • The speed of light, 299,792,458 m/s: exact by the SI definition of the metre (BIPM, SI Brochure, 9th edition).
  • Visible light about 400 to 700 nm, the spectrum from radio to gamma rays, \(c = \lambda f\): OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 5 "Radiation and Spectra" (the book, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), in our own words.

docs.title: 3.2 Hot things glow
docs.text: Unit 3 · Light itself · Lesson 3.2 · 15 min

docs.title: Hot things glow
docs.text:
Lesson 3.1 ended with a promise: cool stars shine mostly in red and infrared light. Here is a star at 3,300 K, a typical red dwarf, drawn colour by colour.

The bottom axis is colour again, as in lesson 3.1. Before reading on, guess: at what wavelength is this star brightest? Is that a colour your eye can see?

docs.title: Everything warm glows
docs.text:
Push a metal poker into a fire. At first it only feels hot. Then it glows dull red, then orange, then yellow-white. Nothing was added to it. It sends out light because it is hot, and the hotter it gets, the more light it sends and the bluer that light becomes.

A star is a ball of gas far hotter than any poker, and it glows for the same reason. Its surface is close to what physicists call a blackbody.

Blackbody. An object whose light comes only from its own heat. The odd name comes from the cold case: a cold one reflects nothing and looks black. Heat it and it glows, in a pattern set by one number, its temperature.

The plot above shows that pattern for 3,300 K. It is a hill: one colour is brightest, and the glow falls away on both sides, quickly on the blue side and slowly on the long-wave side.

docs.title: The rule: hotter means bluer
docs.text:
Raise the temperature and the whole hill slides toward shorter wavelengths. The top of the hill, the peak, follows a simple rule found by Wilhelm Wien in 1893.

Wien's law. The wavelength where a blackbody glows brightest is a constant divided by its temperature. Twice as hot, half the peak wavelength.

\[ \lambda_{\text{peak}} = \frac{b}{T}, \qquad b = 2.898 \times 10^{6} \text{ nm K} \]

Here \(T\) is in kelvin (lesson 2.3) and \(\lambda_{\text{peak}}\) comes out in nanometres. Look at the second plot: the Sun, at 5,772 K.

Its peak is at \(2.898 \times 10^{6} / 5{,}772 = 502\) nm, green. Yet the Sun looks white, not green. The reason is on the plot: at 400 nm the glow is still 0.87 of the peak, and at 700 nm still 0.79. The Sun sends plenty of every colour your eye can see, and the eye adds them up to white.

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
a. One star's glow peaks at 800 nm. A second star is twice as hot. Where does its glow peak, in nm?

b. A 3,000 K star and a 6,000 K star. Which one has the longer peak wavelength: the hotter or the cooler? (One word.)

c. A 3,000 K star peaks at 966 nm. Where does a 9,000 K star peak, in nm?

Worked example: where does a 3,300 K star peak?

Step 1. Divide the constant by the temperature. \(\lambda_{\text{peak}} = 2.898 \times 10^{6} / 3{,}300 = 878\) nm.

Step 2. Where is that? Beyond red. Your eye stops at about 700 nm, so this star's brightest light is infrared, but it sits well inside the band where TESS keeps at least half of its best response (580 to 982 nm, lesson 3.1).

Your turn, half done: a 3,000 K star

Step 1: divide \(2.898 \times 10^{6}\) by \(3{,}000\). Finish, and say whether TESS sees that colour.

Your turn. The peak wavelength of a 3,000 K star, in nm:

Worked solution

\(\lambda_{\text{peak}} = 2.898 \times 10^{6} / 3{,}000 = 966\) nm, infrared. TESS still records at least half of its best response there, so a star this cool is bright to TESS even though it looks dim to your eye.

The rule: \(\lambda_{\text{peak}} = b / T\), with \(T\) in kelvin.

docs.title: One curve, two rules
docs.text:
Lesson 2.3 gave you the brightness rule: each square metre of a hot surface sends out light in proportion to \(T^4\). It is the same hill. The total light is the area under the curve, and when the temperature doubles the hill gets higher everywhere, with an area 16 times larger. Hotter means brighter, and Wien's law says hotter also means bluer. Both rules come from one curve, written down by Max Planck in 1900, and the plots here are drawn from it.

You can run Wien's law backwards, and astronomers do. Measure where a star's glow peaks and you know its temperature, without going near it. A star's colour is its temperature in disguise.

docs.title: Back to the plots
docs.text:
Touch the red dwarf's hill. It peaks at 878 nm, exactly where Wien's law says. Red dwarfs run from about 3,850 K (type M0) to 3,060 K (type M5), so their peaks fall between about 753 and 947 nm. All of them sit inside the colour band TESS records best.

Now the Sun. Its peak, 502 nm, falls where TESS is blind. TESS still sees the Sun's long-wave tail, the glow at 600 to 1,000 nm, but on the plot that tail is only 0.41 to 0.93 of the peak. For a red dwarf the same colours are the top of the hill. That is the plain meaning of lesson 3.1's last paragraph: a red-seeing camera is a camera tuned to the colours cool stars glow in.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: Anything hot glows, and a blackbody's glow is a hill whose peak wavelength is \(b / T\) (Wien's law, \(b = 2.898 \times 10^{6}\) nm K): hotter means a shorter peak, so bluer. The same curve gives the \(T^4\) brightness rule of lesson 2.3 as its area. Red dwarfs, 3,060 to 3,850 K, peak at 750 to 950 nm, inside TESS's band; the Sun peaks at 502 nm, in the colours TESS cannot see.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. Read the second plot, the Sun: about what share of the peak glow is there at 1,000 nm?

Worked solution

About 0.41. Touch the curve at 1,000 nm: the glow has fallen to a bit under half of its value at 502 nm.

2. A hot blue star has a surface at 12,000 K. Where does its glow peak, in nm?

Worked solution

\(2.898 \times 10^{6} / 12{,}000 = 241.5\) nm. That is ultraviolet, shorter than violet (about 400 nm), so neither your eye nor TESS sees the top of its hill. Only the long-wave tail reaches us, and that tail is blue-white to the eye.

3. The coolest star in the red dwarf range of lesson 3.1 is type M5, at 3,060 K. Where does it peak, in nm?

Worked solution

\(2.898 \times 10^{6} / 3{,}060 = 947\) nm. Even the coolest red dwarfs on the list peak inside the 580 to 982 nm band where TESS keeps at least half its best response.

4. A star's glow peaks at 725 nm. What is its temperature, in K? (Run the rule backwards: \(T = b / \lambda_{\text{peak}}\).)

Worked solution

\(T = 2.898 \times 10^{6} / 725 = 3{,}997\) K, about 4,000 K. That is a cool orange-red star, a little warmer than an M0 red dwarf.

5. You glow too. Your skin is about 310 K. Where does your glow peak, in nm?

Worked solution

\(2.898 \times 10^{6} / 310 = 9{,}348\) nm, about 9.3 micrometres: far into the infrared. Your eye cannot see it, but a thermal camera is built to, which is why it shows warm bodies glowing in the dark.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:

The script checks that the top of each curve lands where Wien's law puts it: 878.1 nm at 3,300 K and 502.0 nm at 5,772 K (read 17 Nov 2026).
  • Wien's law and its constant \(b = 2.897771955 \times 10^{-3}\) m K: NIST CODATA 2018 value of the Wien wavelength displacement law constant; the idea, blackbodies, Planck's law and the area under the curve: OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 5 "Radiation and Spectra" (the book, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), in our own words. The dates 1893 (Wien) and 1900 (Planck) are the textbook dates.
  • The Sun's 5,772 K: the IAU 2015 nominal solar effective temperature (Resolution B3, Prsa et al. 2016, AJ 152, 41); the 5,770 K in Mamajek's table below agrees.
  • Star temperatures by type, M0 dwarf 3,850 K, M5 dwarf 3,060 K, G2 dwarf 5,770 K: E. Mamajek, "A Modern Mean Dwarf Stellar Color and Effective Temperature Sequence", version 2022.04.16 (table, downloaded 17 Nov 2026, based on Pecaut and Mamajek 2013, ApJS 208, 9). The 3,300 K red dwarf is a made-up mid-range example, not a named star.
  • TESS band and red dwarfs: lesson 3.1 and Ricker et al. 2015 (arXiv 1406.0151).

docs.title: 3.3 Fingerprints
docs.text: Unit 3 · Light itself · Lesson 3.3 · 16 min

docs.title: Fingerprints
docs.text:
Lesson 3.2 drew a star's glow as a smooth hill. Here is the real thing: the light of one star, split into its colours by an instrument called a spectrograph.

The hill is there, but it is full of narrow dark gaps. Before reading on, guess: what could take away exactly one colour of a star's light and leave the colours on both sides?

docs.title: A spectrum with gaps
docs.text:
This star is hot, about 9,700 K, so by Wien's law its hill peaks near 299 nm, off the left edge of the plot. What you see is the downhill side, running from violet to red, with dark gaps cut into it. The gaps sit near 656, 486, 434, 410 and 397 nm, and more, crowding closer together toward the blue end.

Absorption line. A narrow range of wavelengths where a star's light is missing. The opposite, a bright line on a dark background, is an emission line: the glow of a thin hot gas.

Something between the star's hot glowing layers and your telescope is swallowing those exact colours. It is the star's own thin outer gas, and it swallows light in a pattern that depends on what atoms the gas is made of.

docs.title: Why only certain colours: the ladder
docs.text:
An electron in an atom cannot have just any amount of energy. It can sit only on certain "rungs", like a ladder with no standing room between the steps. A photon, one packet of light, can lift the electron from one rung to a higher one only if the photon's energy equals the gap between the rungs exactly. Too little or too much and the photon passes by.

A photon's energy comes from its wavelength. For atoms the handy unit is the electronvolt.

Electronvolt (eV). A tiny unit of energy, the size used for single atoms and single photons. A photon of wavelength \(\lambda\) carries \(E = 1{,}240 / \lambda\) electronvolts when \(\lambda\) is in nanometres. Visible light, 700 to 400 nm, carries about 1.8 to 3.1 eV.

Hydrogen is the simplest atom, one electron, and its rungs are known exactly: rung number \(n\) (1, 2, 3, and so on) sits at \(-13.6 / n^{2}\) eV. Take an electron sitting on rung 2. Lifting it to rung 3 costs \(13.6 \times (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89\) eV, which is a photon of \(1{,}240 / 1.89 = 656\) nm: red. Lifting it to rung 4 costs 2.55 eV, a photon of 486 nm. Every jump from rung 2 up to a higher rung \(n\) takes one fixed colour, and together they are the Balmer lines of hydrogen. Johann Balmer found their pattern in 1885, long before anyone knew about rungs. Written as a rule for the wavelength:

\[ \frac{1}{\lambda} = R \left( \frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{n^{2}} \right), \qquad R = 1.0968 \times 10^{7} \text{ per metre} \]

(\(R\) is the Rydberg constant for hydrogen.) As \(n\) grows, the lines crowd together and stop at a limit, the end of the series.

docs.title: Think it through
docs.text:
a. A photon of orange light has a wavelength of 620 nm. Using \(E = 1{,}240 / \lambda\), what is its energy, in eV?

b. A photon of 656 nm light or a photon of 486 nm light: which carries more energy? (Type the wavelength.)

Worked example: the wavelength of the \(n = 3\) line

Step 1. The bracket. \(1/4 - 1/9 = 9/36 - 4/36 = 5/36 = 0.1389\).

Step 2. Multiply by \(R\). \(1/\lambda = 1.0968 \times 10^{7} \times 0.1389 = 1.523 \times 10^{6}\) per metre.

Step 3. Turn it over and convert. \(\lambda = 1 / 1.523 \times 10^{6} = 6.565 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 656.5\) nm.

This is H-alpha, the red line, the first of the Balmer lines.

Your turn, half done: the \(n = 4\) line

Step 1: \(1/4 - 1/16 = 3/16 = 0.1875\). Finish: multiply by \(R\), turn it over, and convert to nanometres.

Your turn. The wavelength of the \(n = 4\) Balmer line, in nm:

Worked solution

\(1/\lambda = 1.0968 \times 10^{7} \times 0.1875 = 2.0565 \times 10^{6}\) per metre, so \(\lambda = 4.863 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 486.3\) nm. This is H-beta, blue-green.

The rule: \(1/\lambda = R\,(1/4 - 1/n^{2})\), then turn it over.

docs.title: Back to the plot
docs.text:
Touch the dips on the star's spectrum. The darkest points sit at 656.45, 486.30, 434.21, 410.30 and 397.10 nm. The formula, which knows nothing about this star, says 656.47, 486.27, 434.17, 410.29 and 397.12. For all seven lines from \(n = 3\) to \(n = 9\) the formula and the file agree within 0.05 nm. The dark gaps in a star's light are hydrogen, and an atom's ladder predicts exactly where.

Why does this star show hydrogen so strongly? At about 9,700 K the gas is hot enough that many hydrogen atoms sit on rung 2, the starting rung for the Balmer lines, but not so hot that the atoms lose their electrons altogether. In cooler stars most atoms sit on rung 1, whose lines are in the ultraviolet, and in much hotter stars hydrogen is stripped bare. The strength of the lines is therefore a second thermometer.

docs.title: Every atom has its own fingerprint
docs.text:
Each kind of atom has its own ladder, so its own set of wavelengths. Sodium has a pair near 589 nm, the orange-yellow of old street lamps. Helium has a line near 588 nm. Iron has thousands. Match the dark lines in a star's spectrum to the laboratory lines of each atom and you can read what the star's outer gas is made of, from a distance no spacecraft could cross.

In 1925 Cecilia Payne did exactly that, with thousands of spectra and laboratory data, and found that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. The senior astronomer on her thesis committee disagreed, she added a line to her thesis doubting her own result, and later studies confirmed it.

docs.title: Why this matters for Second Sun
docs.text: TESS adds up every colour it can record into a single number each moment (lesson 3.1). The H-alpha dip at 656 nm sits inside TESS's band, but TESS cannot pull it apart from the colours around it. A light curve has no fingerprints, only the total brightness. Lines are a different kind of data, and lesson 3.4 uses them to measure speeds.

docs.title: In a few sentences
docs.text: An electron in an atom can sit only on certain rungs, so an atom takes in only photons whose energy (\(E = 1{,}240 / \lambda\) eV, with \(\lambda\) in nm) matches a gap between rungs. That cuts dark absorption lines into a star's spectrum at wavelengths set by its atoms. Hydrogen's Balmer lines follow \(1/\lambda = R\,(1/4 - 1/n^{2})\) and match a real star's spectrum to 0.05 nm. TESS's single brightness number hides all of this.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
1. Touch the plot near 486 nm. Which Balmer line is that dip? (H-alpha, H-beta, H-gamma, and so on.)

Worked solution

H-beta, the \(n = 4\) line, at 486 nm. The series goes H-alpha (656 nm), H-beta (486), H-gamma (434), H-delta (410).

2. Predict the \(n = 5\) Balmer line. What wavelength, in nm?

Worked solution

\(1/4 - 1/25 = 0.21\), \(1/\lambda = 1.0968 \times 10^{7} \times 0.21 = 2.303 \times 10^{6}\) per metre, \(\lambda = 4.342 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 434.2\) nm. On the plot, the dip is at 434.21 nm: H-gamma.

3. As \(n\) gets very large, \(1/n^{2}\) shrinks to almost nothing. Where do the Balmer lines pile up, in nm? (Use \(\lambda = 4 / R\).)

Worked solution

\(\lambda = 4 / (1.0968 \times 10^{7}) = 3.647 \times 10^{-7}\) m \(= 364.7\) nm, the series limit. Every Balmer line lies between 656 nm and this limit, and they bunch up toward it. That is why the left edge of the plot is crowded with dips.

4. Find the energy of an H-alpha photon (656.5 nm) two ways: from the wavelength, \(E = 1{,}240 / \lambda\). Does it match the rung gap \(13.6 \times (1/4 - 1/9) = 1.89\) eV? Give the first answer, in eV.

Worked solution

\(E = 1{,}240 / 656.5 = 1.889\) eV. Both routes give 1.89 eV. That agreement is the whole idea: the colour of a line and the size of the gap between two rungs are the same fact written two ways.

5. Could a TESS light curve of this star show you its hydrogen dips? (Yes or no.)

Worked solution

No. TESS records one brightness number for all the colours it sees at once. The H-alpha dip is a tiny gap in one colour, so it is lost in the total. To see lines you must first split the light by colour, which a spectrograph does and TESS does not.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• The spectrum: SDSS DR17 spectrum of an A0 star, plate 2938, MJD 54526, fibre 518, from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (Abdurro'uf et al. 2022, ApJS 259, 35; the survey); chosen from the survey catalogue as a bright A0 star whose motion is too small to move its lines (redshift 2.6e-6, 0.8 km/s). File downloaded 17 Nov 2026 (research/downloads.csv). The star is not cross-matched against our hunt lists, and no TESS light of it is used. SDSS wavelengths are in vacuum, and so are the formula's.
  • The check against the formula, our own script book/tools/lesson_plots_u3b.py (17 Nov 2026): the darkest point of the file near each predicted line sits within 0.05 nm of it for \(n = 3\) to \(9\) (656.45 against 656.47, 486.30 against 486.27, 434.21 against 434.17, 410.30 against 410.29, 397.10 against 397.12 nm).
  • The Rydberg constant \(R_H = 1.0967758 \times 10^{7}\) per metre: the NIST CODATA value for infinite mass, \(10{,}973{,}731.568\) per metre, corrected for the proton's finite mass. The ladder, photon energy, Balmer series, absorption and emission lines: OpenStax Astronomy 2e, chapter 5 "Radiation and Spectra" (the book, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), in our own words. Balmer 1885 is the textbook date.
  • The star's temperature, about 9,700 K, from the type A0 dwarf row of Mamajek's table (lesson 3.2 sources). That Balmer lines are strongest in A stars near this temperature: OpenStax, same chapter.
  • Cecilia Payne's 1925 thesis, its result, and her committee's doubt: Science History Institute, "Cecilia Payne-Gaposchkin" (biography, read 17 Nov 2026). The thesis is "Stellar Atmospheres" (Harvard, 1925).

docs.title: For astronomers
docs.text:
Reference · about 3 min · written 27 Oct 2026

In plain words

Second Sun is a small citizen-science project that looks for planets orbiting two stars in public TESS data. It has found no planet and claims none. This page says what is solid, what is not yet, and where to check each statement.

docs.title: Who writes this
docs.text: The book is by Ahmed Hanzala, an independent citizen scientist who is learning astronomy as the project goes, with Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic. Claude writes most of the code and the diary-style text and runs the checks. Ahmed decides what to test, reads the results, and is the human second key on any candidate: both keys must turn before anything leaves the project. Because the book is a diary written to Ahmed, it speaks to "you".

docs.title: What has been done
docs.text:
Every line below has a label and a source on the facts page; the claim number is in brackets.

  • Known planets. 14 transiting two-star planets are known: 12 from Kepler and 2 from TESS (F-001).
  • The detector. It flattens each light curve, bins it to 10 minutes and scans boxes 3 to 15 hours long (Chapter 8). It re-found the known planet TOI-1338 b in 4 of the 8 sectors with data at the transit; the missed transits had a signal strength of 3.7 to 6.5 (F-014).
  • Honest false alarms. The same search runs on upside-down copies of the data to count how often noise alone crosses the bar (Chapter 9).
  • How faint is too faint. We hid six fake two-star planets (33 crossings) in 40 sectors of TOI-1338. The search found 0 of 10 at 4 Earth radii, 8 of 10 at 6 and 10 of 10 at 8 (F-029).
  • The professionals' tool. We ran STANLEY (Martin and Fabrycky 2021) on TOI-1338. Its best score was 18.4 sigma at 96.11 days, but 28% of all orbits it tried scored above 5 sigma, so its sigma scale is not calibrated (F-045). We say so wherever we mention that number (Chapter 12).

docs.title: What we do not claim
docs.text:
• No planet and no candidate. The hunt on the real target list is on hold, as of 27 Oct 2026.
  • No new method. The methods are published; our contribution so far is an open, labelled record of using them, mistakes included (Chapter 15).
  • Nothing below those limits. In our injection test, no planet of 4 Earth radii was found.
  • NASA's ExoFOP takes candidates only after a paper, so we would publish first (Chapter 14).

docs.title: How to check us
docs.text:
• Every number on the facts page carries a label (VERIFIED, LIKELY, UNCERTAIN or NOT TESTED) and a source. If you find one that is wrong, we want to know.
  • The code, the data tables and the tests are public: github.com/M1Smacker/second-sun (MIT licence). Open an issue there.
  • The prior work page says how this project relates to the published searches.
  • The reading list shows how deeply we have read each paper.

docs.title: Prior work and how we differ
docs.text:
Reference · about 4 min · written 27 Oct 2026

In plain words

Other teams have already searched TESS for planets that orbit two stars, with published methods and peer review. This page lists the ones we know, says how deeply we have read each, and says honestly where this project is different and where it is not.

docs.title: The published searches we know
docs.text:
Work What it did How we read it Davies et al. 2026, MNRAS 548 (arXiv:2604.09435), a Warwick team A semi-automated search for single transits (the tool is called mono-cbp). It searched 512 detached eclipsing binaries with orbits over 7 days and reported one weak candidate. An event was kept only if it survived at least 18 of 21 different detrendings (F-021). abstract; Table 2 (F-001) Paz 2024, AJ (arXiv:2409.15499) and Paz and others 2026 (arXiv:2605.19059) VARnet and VarWISE: a machine-learning detector and a catalogue of 1.9 million infrared variable objects from NEOWISE. Not a planet search: it has no planet class and sparse six-month epochs. abstracts and most of the text, not the final sections Thornton et al. 2026, MNRAS 548 (arXiv:2512.07934) 27 candidate two-star planets from the slow turning of the binary's orbit (apsidal precession), found by timing eclipses, not by looking for transits. title only Oddo et al. 2026 (arXiv:2610.22625) The occurrence of two-star planets around red-dwarf eclipsing binaries in TESS. An earlier conference abstract, "Towards Transiting Tatooines" (2024), described the search. title only Martin and Fabrycky 2021, AJ 162, 84 STANLEY: stack shallow crossings that do not keep time, using simulated orbits. abstract; we ran it (F-044, F-045)

"Title only" means we confirmed the paper exists and what it is called, and nothing more. We will not describe results we have not read.

docs.title: How this project is different, as far as we know
docs.text:
• Different list. Our list is 549 Kepler eclipsing binaries, looked at again in TESS data. Davies et al. used TESS-selected binaries, Thornton et al. used Gaia binaries, and Oddo et al. used red-dwarf binaries. How many of our stars are also in Davies et al.'s 512 we have not measured yet.
  • Different method from Thornton et al. They time the eclipses; we look for the planet's own dips. The two approaches are complementary, and a star that shows up in both would be interesting.
  • Same kind of method as Davies et al., built separately. Both look for dips in detrended light curves. We have not used their code in any result, and we have not compared the two detectors on the same stars.
  • What is new is small. An open, labelled record of every step, mistakes included; two keys on every candidate, one of them human; and a book that teaches the method. No new science yet.

docs.title: What we depend on
docs.text: The published searches above, STANLEY's published code (MIT licence), and NASA's public TESS and Kepler data. If you notice something we have misread or left out, please open an issue.
